nodes.name: Free linear quantum Liouville equation
nodes.statement: \left\{ \begin{array}{l} i \partial_t u=\big[-\Delta,u \big]+\varrho,\\ u(t=0)=u_0, \end{array} \right.
nodes.label: liou

nodes.name: Smoothness condition on the initial density operator
nodes.statement: \textrm{Tr} \left((\mathbb{I}-\Delta)^{\beta/2} (u_0)^2 (\mathbb{I}-\Delta)^{\beta/2}\right)^p < \infty
nodes.label: regu0

nodes.name: Homogeneous/non-homogeneous decomposition and localized operators
nodes.statement: \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \displaystyle \Upsilon(t):=e^{i t \Delta} \,u_0\, e^{-i t\Delta}, &\qquad \displaystyle \Gamma(t):=\int_0^t e^{i (t-s) \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{-i (t-s) \Delta} ds\\ \displaystyle \sigma_\beta(t) := \chi_t\, \Lambda_\beta\, \Upsilon(t)\, \Lambda_\beta\, \chi_t, &\qquad \displaystyle \gamma_\beta(t) := \chi_t\, \Lambda_\beta\, \Gamma(t)\, \Lambda_\beta\, \chi_t, \end{array} \right.
nodes.label: defop

nodes.name: Formal local densities of sigma_beta and gamma_beta
nodes.statement: n_{\sigma_\beta}= \sum_{j \in \mathbb N} \lambda_j | \chi_t \Lambda_\beta \psi_j |^2, \qquad n_{\gamma_\beta}= \sum_{j \in \mathbb N} \mu_j | \chi_t \Lambda_\beta \phi_j|^2.
nodes.label: defn

nodes.name: Local density estimates
nodes.statement: \|n_{\sigma_\beta}\|_{L^{r/2}(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \leq C_\chi \|u_0\|_{\mathcal J_p}, \qquad \|n_{\gamma_\beta}\|_{L^{r/2}(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \leq C_\chi \|\varrho\|_{L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_p)},
nodes.label: estnth

nodes.name: Trace class estimates on sigma_beta and gamma_beta
nodes.statement: \|\sigma_\beta\|_{L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_1)} \leq C_\chi \|u_0\|_{\mathcal J_p}, \qquad \|\gamma_\beta\|_{L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_1)} \leq C_\chi \|\varrho\|_{L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_p)}.
nodes.label: esttraceth

nodes.name: Parameter constraints of Lemma 2.7
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{l} \displaystyle 2\alpha+\beta < \frac{(d+1)}{r}-\frac{d}{2}, \qquad \textrm{if} \qquad r\in (2,\infty),\\ \displaystyle 2\alpha+\beta \leq \frac{1}{2}, \qquad \textrm{if} \qquad r =2. \end{array} \right.
nodes.label: conslem

nodes.name: Smoothness condition on rho
nodes.statement: \int_{\mathbb R} dt\, \textrm{Tr} \Big((1+|x|^k) (-\Delta)^n \,\varrho(t)\, (-\Delta)^n (1+|x|^k)\Big) <\infty, \quad \forall k,n \in \mathbb N.
nodes.label: condrho

nodes.name: Justification of Fubini by a trace bound
nodes.statement: &\int_0^t ds \,\left|\textrm{Tr} \left( \chi_t \Lambda_{\beta}e^{i(t- s) \Delta} \varrho(s)e^{-i (t-s) \Delta }\Lambda_{\beta}\chi_t \, \varphi_t \right)\right| \\ \nonumber &\hspace{2cm}=\int_0^t ds \,\left|\textrm{Tr} \left( \chi_t e^{i(t- s) \Delta} \Lambda_{\beta} \varrho(s)\Lambda_{\beta} e^{-i (t-s) \Delta }\chi_t \, \varphi_t \right)\right| \\ \nonumber &\hspace{2cm} \leq \|\chi_t\|^2_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \|\varphi_t \|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \int_{\mathbb R} ds\, \| \Lambda_{\beta} \varrho(s) \Lambda_{\beta} \|_{\mathcal J_1} < \infty.
nodes.label: justi

nodes.name: Parameter conditions for Theorem 2.1 (first inequality)
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{l} \displaystyle \beta < \frac{1+d}{r}-\frac{d}{2} \qquad \textrm{if} \qquad 1 \leq r' <2, \qquad \\ \displaystyle \beta\leq \frac{1}{2} \qquad \textrm{if} \qquad r'=2. \end{array} \right.
nodes.label: eqq1

nodes.name: Parameter conditions for the dual estimate
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{l} \displaystyle \beta < \frac{1+d}{r' q}-\frac{d}{2} \qquad \textrm{if} \qquad 2< r'q <\infty, \qquad \\ \displaystyle \beta\leq \frac{1}{2} \qquad \textrm{if} \qquad r'q=2. \end{array} \right.
nodes.label: eqq2

nodes.name: Bound on II(s)
nodes.statement: \nonumber |II(s)|&=&\left|\textrm{Tr} \, \left( J_\alpha^{-1} e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{is \Delta} (J_\alpha^*)^{-1}J_\alpha^* F_\beta(s) J_\alpha \right) \right|\\ &\leq & \textrm{Tr} \, \left( J_\alpha^{-1} e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{is \Delta} (J_\alpha^*)^{-1} \right) \| J_\alpha^* F_\beta(s) J_\alpha \|.
nodes.label: T2

nodes.name: Estimate of J_1
nodes.statement: \| J_1\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)} \leq C \|t^\alpha \phi_t\|_{L^{r'}((-T,T)\times \mathbb R^{d})} \leq C \|\phi_t\|_{L^{r'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})},
nodes.label: estJ1

nodes.name: Main constraint on alpha and beta
nodes.statement: \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \displaystyle 2\alpha+\beta < \frac{(d+1)}{r}-\frac{d}{2}, \qquad r'\in [1,2).\\ \displaystyle 2\alpha+\beta \leq \frac{1}{2}, \qquad r'=2. \end{array} \right.
nodes.label: mainconst

nodes.name: Integral representation of the fractional Laplacian
nodes.statement: D^\alpha(\varphi)(x)=c_{d,\alpha} \int_{\mathbb R^d} \frac{\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)}{|x-y|^{d+\alpha}} dy.
nodes.label: locfrac

nodes.name: Estimate of J_2
nodes.statement: \| J_2\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)} \leq C \|R_{t,1}+R_{t,2}\|_{L^{q'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})},\; \textrm{with} \; \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \displaystyle \alpha+\beta < \frac{(d+1)}{q}-\frac{d}{2}, \quad q'\in [1,2).\\ \displaystyle \alpha+\beta \leq \frac{1}{2}, \quad q'=2. \end{array} \right.
nodes.label: estJ2

nodes.name: Elementary bound on 1-exp(i(|x|^2-|y|^2)/4t)
nodes.statement: \left| 1- e^{i\frac{|x|^2-|y|^2}{4t}}\right| \leq 2^{1-3a}t^{-a} |x+y|^a|x-y|^a\leq 2^{1-3a}t^{-a}\left( 2^a|y|^a|x-y|^{a} +|x-y|^{2a}\right).
nodes.label: AF

nodes.name: Constraints on s and epsilon
nodes.statement: 1<\frac{s d}{d-\varepsilon s} < 2, \qquad \alpha+\beta < \left(\frac{1}{s'}+\frac{\varepsilon}{d}\right)(d+1)-\frac{d}{2}, \qquad r<s'<\infty.
nodes.label: const

nodes.name: Chain of bounds on R_{t,3}
nodes.statement: \nonumber \|R_{t,3}\|_{L^{q'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})} &\leq& C\| t^{-\varepsilon} (1+|x|^{1+\alpha+\varepsilon}) u_t \|_{L^{q'}(\mathbb R_t,L^{s}(\mathbb R_x^{d}))} \\\nonumber &\leq& C\| t^{-\varepsilon} u_t \|_{L^{q'}(\mathbb R_t,L^{r'}(\mathbb R_x^{d}))}\\ &\leq& C\left(\int_{-T}^T t^{-\varepsilon q' p' } \right)^{1/(q'p')} \|\phi_t\|_{L^{r'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})},
nodes.label: intT

nodes.name: Constraint p>1
nodes.statement: p=\frac{r'}{q'}=\frac{(d-\varepsilon s)r'}{sd} > 1, \qquad i.e. \qquad 1<s<\frac{dr'}{d+\varepsilon r'}.
nodes.label: eqp

nodes.name: Integrability condition in time
nodes.statement: \varepsilon q' p'=\frac{\varepsilon r'sd}{r'(d-\varepsilon s)-sd}<1, \qquad i.e. \qquad sr'\varepsilon (d+1)+sd<dr'.
nodes.label: est4

nodes.name: Constraints in terms of delta
nodes.statement: r' (r'-\delta) \varepsilon (d+1)<\delta d, \qquad \frac{1}{2} < \frac{1}{r'-\delta}-\frac{\varepsilon}{d}.
nodes.label: const5

nodes.name: Constraints on epsilon and alpha+beta
nodes.statement: 0<\varepsilon\leq 1-\alpha, \qquad \alpha+\beta < \left(\frac{1}{s'}+\frac{\varepsilon}{d}\right)(d+1)-\frac{d}{2}.
nodes.label: const3

nodes.name: Constraint on delta
nodes.statement: \frac{\delta}{r'(r'-\delta)} \leq \frac{\varepsilon}{d}+\frac{\alpha}{d+1}=\frac{\delta }{4(d+1)}+\frac{\alpha}{d+1}.
nodes.label: const22

nodes.name: Bound on D^beta n^v
nodes.statement: \nonumber \|D^\beta n^v\|_{L^{\frac{d}{d-\beta}}(\mathbb R_x^d)}&\leq& C \left\| \left(\sum_{j\in \mathbb N} \mu_j |\phi^v_j|^2\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_{j\in \mathbb N} \mu_j |D^\beta(\phi^v_j)|^2\right)^{1/2} \right\|_{L^{\frac{d}{d-\beta}}(\mathbb R^d_x)}\\ && \qquad +C \sum_{j\in \mathbb N} \mu_j\big\|\mathcal D_{\beta/2}(\phi_j^v) \big\|_{L^{\frac{2d}{d-\beta}}(\mathbb R^d_x)}^2.
nodes.label: Dn

nodes.name: Density operator
nodes.statement: The main object of interest is the \textit{density operator}, denoted by $u$ in the sequel, which is in general a trace class, self-adjoint and nonnegative operator on some Hilbert space (here $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$, where $d\geq 1$ is dimension).
nodes.genus: trace class, self-adjoint and nonnegative operator on some Hilbert space

nodes.name: Quantum Liouville equation (von Neumann equation)
nodes.statement: With physical constants set to one, the free, linear Liouville equation reads \begin{equation} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} i \partial_t u=\big[-\Delta,u \big]+\varrho,\\ u(t=0)=u_0, \end{array} \right. \end{equation} where $u_0$ and $\varrho$ are given operators, $[\cdot, \cdot]$ denotes commutator between operators and $\Delta$ is the usual Laplacian on $\mathbb R^d$.
nodes.statement_short: The free linear quantum Liouville equation $i\partial_t u=[-\Delta,u]+\varrho$, $u(0)=u_0$, for operators $u_0,\varrho$.

nodes.name: Lieb-Thirring inequalities
nodes.statement: \textit{The Lieb-Thirring inequalities \cite{LT,LP}.} They are the density operator counterpart of Gagliardo-Nirenberg-Sobolev inequalities: for $u_0$ as before, if we define formally the local density $n_{u_0}$ and the local kinetic energy $\mathcal E_{u_0}$ by $$ n_{u_0}:=\sum_{j \in \mathbb N} \lambda_j |u_j|^2, \qquad \mathcal E_{u_0}:=\sum_{j \in \mathbb N} \lambda_j |\nabla u_j|^2, $$ an example of such inequalities is $$ \|n_{u_0}\|_{L^q(\mathbb R^d)} \leq C \left(\sum_{j \in \mathbb N} \lambda_j^p \right)^{\theta/p} \|\mathcal E_{u_0}\|^{1-\theta}_{L^1(\mathbb R^d)} $$ where $p \in [1,\infty]$ and $$ \theta=\frac{2p}{(d+2)p-d}, \qquad q=\frac{(d+2)p-d}{dp-(d-2)}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Lieb-Thirring: the $L^q$ norm of the local density is bounded by Schatten norms of $u_0$ times the kinetic energy to a power.

nodes.name: Strichartz inequalities for orthonormal systems
nodes.statement: \textit{The Strichartz inequalities \cite{LewStri,FrankSabin}.} They are generalizations to orthonormal systems of the classical Strichartz estimates for the Schr\"odinger equation, and read, see \cite{FrankSabin}, Theorem 8, $$ \left\|\sum_{j \in \mathbb N} \lambda_j |e^{i t\Delta}u_j|^2 \right\|_{L^p_tL^q_x(\mathbb R\times \mathbb R^d)} \leq \left( \sum_{j \in \mathbb N} \lambda_j^{\frac{2q}{q+1}}\right)^{\frac{q+1}{2q}},$$ with $p,q,d \geq 1$, $$ \frac{2}{p}+\frac{d}{q}=d, \qquad 1 \leq q <1+\frac{2}{d-1}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Strichartz estimates for orthonormal systems: $L^p_tL^q_x$ norm of $\sum\lambda_j|e^{it\Delta}u_j|^2$ bounded by an $\ell^{2q/(q+1)}$ norm of $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Local smoothing effect for the Schrodinger equation
nodes.statement: We are interested in the \textit{local smoothing effect} discovered by Constantin and Saut \cite{ConstSaut}, Sjolin \cite{sjolin} and Vega \cite{vega}: if $v_0 \in L^2(\mathbb R^d)$, then $v=e^{it\Delta}v_0$ admits locally spatial fractional derivatives of order $1/2$.
conclusions: $v=e^{it\Delta}v_0$ admits locally spatial fractional derivatives of order $1/2$

nodes.name: Fourier transforms F_x and F
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathcal F_x$ the Fourier transform with respect to the $x \in \mathbb R^d$ variable, and by $\mathcal F$ the Fourier transform with respect to $(t,x)$, with the convention $$ \mathcal F_x \varphi(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{-i x \cdot \xi} \, \varphi(x) dx. $$

nodes.name: Bessel potential Lambda_beta and fractional Laplacian D^beta
nodes.statement: For $\beta \in \mathbb R$, let $\Lambda_\beta:=(\mathbb{I}-\Delta)^{\beta/2}$, and let $D^\beta:=(-\Delta)^{\beta/2}$ be the fractional Laplacian, that we will only consider for $\beta \in (0,1/2]$. The operator $\Lambda_\beta$ and $D^\beta$ are defined in the Fourier space as pseudo-differential operators with symbols $(1+|\xi|^2)^{\beta/2}$ and $|\xi|^{\beta}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Lambda_\beta=(I-\Delta)^{\beta/2}$ and the fractional Laplacian $D^\beta=(-\Delta)^{\beta/2}$, Fourier multipliers.

nodes.name: Conjugate exponent
nodes.statement: We systematically use $r'$ for the conjugate exponent of $r \in [1,\infty]$ defined as usual by $\frac{1}{r}+\frac{1}{r'}=1$.

nodes.name: Potential space H^{beta,p}
nodes.statement: For $\beta \in \mathbb R$ and $p\in[1,\infty]$, we will use the potential space $H^{\beta,p}(\mathbb R^d)$ defined by $H^{\beta,p}(\mathbb R^d)=\{ \varphi \in \mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d), \Lambda_\beta \varphi \in L^p(\mathbb R^d) \}$ with norm $\| \cdot \|_{H^{\beta,p}(\mathbb R^d)}=\| \Lambda_\beta \cdot \|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)}$, where $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$ is the space of tempered distributions on $\mathbb R^d$.

nodes.name: Schwartz space and C_0^infty
nodes.statement: We denote as well by $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ the Schwartz space and by $C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ the space of infinitely differentiable functions on $\mathbb R^d$ with compact support.

nodes.name: Bounded operators on L^2
nodes.statement: The space of bounded operators on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ is denoted by $\mathcal L(L^2(\mathbb R^d))$ and its associated norm is $\| \cdot \|$.

nodes.name: Schatten spaces
nodes.statement: The Schatten spaces on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ are denoted by $\mathcal J_p$, $p \in [1,\infty]$ with the convention $\mathcal J_\infty=\mathcal L(L^2(\mathbb R^d))$.

nodes.name: Decomposition u = Upsilon + Gamma and localized operators sigma_beta, gamma_beta
nodes.statement: We decompose the solution $u$ to {\rm (\ref{liou})} into homogeneous and non-homogeneous parts as $u=\Upsilon+\Gamma$ with \begin{equation} \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \displaystyle \Upsilon(t):=e^{i t \Delta} \,u_0\, e^{-i t\Delta}, &\qquad \displaystyle \Gamma(t):=\int_0^t e^{i (t-s) \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{-i (t-s) \Delta} ds\\ \displaystyle \sigma_\beta(t) := \chi_t\, \Lambda_\beta\, \Upsilon(t)\, \Lambda_\beta\, \chi_t, &\qquad \displaystyle \gamma_\beta(t) := \chi_t\, \Lambda_\beta\, \Gamma(t)\, \Lambda_\beta\, \chi_t, \end{array} \right. \end{equation} where $\chi_t \equiv \chi(t,x) \in C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})$, $u_0 \in \mathcal J_p$, $\varrho \in L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_p)$, and $u_0,\varrho$ are self-adjoint operators.
nodes.statement_short: Split $u=\Upsilon+\Gamma$ into free and Duhamel parts and localize them as $\sigma_\beta=\chi_t\Lambda_\beta\Upsilon\Lambda_\beta\chi_t$, $\gamma_\beta$ likewise.

nodes.name: Well-posedness of the Liouville equation in J_p
nodes.statement: It is then a classical matter that $u$ is the unique mild solution to {\rm (\ref{liou})} and belongs to $C^0(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_p)$.
conclusions: $u$ is the unique mild solution to {\rm (\ref{liou})} and belongs to $C^0(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_p)$

nodes.name: Formal local densities n_{sigma_beta}, n_{gamma_beta}
nodes.statement: Assuming that $\Upsilon, \Gamma \in C^0(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_p)$ admit the decompositions $$ \Upsilon=\sum_{j \in \mathbb N} \lambda_j \ket{\psi_j} \bra{\psi_j}, \qquad \Gamma=\sum_{j \in \mathbb N} \mu_j \ket{\phi_j} \bra{\phi_j}, $$ where $\lambda_j$ and $\mu_j$ are real and $(\psi_i,\psi_j)_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}=(\phi_i,\phi_j)_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}=\delta_{ij}$, we define formally the local densities of $\sigma_\beta$ and $\gamma_\beta$ by \begin{equation} n_{\sigma_\beta}= \sum_{j \in \mathbb N} \lambda_j | \chi_t \Lambda_\beta \psi_j |^2, \qquad n_{\gamma_\beta}= \sum_{j \in \mathbb N} \mu_j | \chi_t \Lambda_\beta \phi_j|^2. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Local density of a trace class operator
nodes.statement: For a trace class operator $u$, the local density $n_u$ is defined rigorously by duality by $$ \int_{\mathbb R^d} n_u(x) \varphi(x) dx=\textrm{Tr} \big( u \varphi \big), \qquad \forall \varphi \in L^\infty(\mathbb R^d), $$ where the multiplication operator by $\varphi$ and the function $\varphi$ are identified (this will be systematically done in the sequel).

nodes.name: Constantin-Saut local smoothing estimate
nodes.statement: Let $q,r' \in [1,2]$, $\beta>0$ such that $$ \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \displaystyle \beta<\frac{1}{r}-d\left(\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{r}\right), \quad \textrm{if}\qquad r\geq 2, \quad r>q\\ \beta \leq \frac{1}{2}\quad \textrm{if}\qquad r=q=2. \end{array} \right. $$ Then, for $\chi_t \equiv \chi \in C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})$, $\varphi_t \equiv \varphi \in \mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d+1})$, the following estimate holds $$ \left(\int_{\mathbb R^d} (1+|\xi|^2)^{\beta q /2} |\mathcal F(\chi_t \varphi_t)(-|\xi|^2,\xi)|^q d\xi \right)^{1/q} \leq C_\chi \| \varphi_t\|_{L^{r'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})}. $$ The constant $C_\chi$ above depends on $\chi$ but not on $\varphi$.
nodes.statement_short: Constantin-Saut: weighted $L^q$ norm of $\mathcal F(\chi\varphi)$ on the paraboloid $\tau=-|\xi|^2$ is bounded by $\|\varphi\|_{L^{r'}}$.
assumptions: Let $q,r' \in [1,2]$, $\beta>0$ such that $$ \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \displaystyle \beta<\frac{1}{r}-d\left(\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{r}\right), \quad \textrm{if}\qquad r\geq 2, \quad r>q\\ \beta \leq \frac{1}{2}\quad \textrm{if}\qquad r=q=2. \end{array} \right. $$
conclusions: the following estimate holds $$ \left(\int_{\mathbb R^d} (1+|\xi|^2)^{\beta q /2} |\mathcal F(\chi_t \varphi_t)(-|\xi|^2,\xi)|^q d\xi \right)^{1/q} \leq C_\chi \| \varphi_t\|_{L^{r'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})}. $$
The constant $C_\chi$ above depends on $\chi$ but not on $\varphi$.
nodes.label: thCS

nodes.name: Dual form of the Constantin-Saut estimate
nodes.statement: We will also use the dual form of Theorem \ref{thCS}. Under the same hypotheses as above, we have $$ \left(\int_{\mathbb R^{d+1}} |\chi(t,x)|^r |\Lambda_\beta e^{it \Delta}\varphi(x) |^r dtdx \right)^{1/r} \leq C_\chi \|\varphi\|_{L^{q}(\mathbb R^{d})}, $$ which shows the local gain of a derivative of order $\beta$.
nodes.statement_short: By duality, $\|\chi\Lambda_\beta e^{it\Delta}\varphi\|_{L^r_{t,x}}\le C\|\varphi\|_{L^q}$: local gain of $\beta$ derivatives.
nodes.label: remdual

nodes.name: Weaker cut-off suffices in Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: It is known that the condition $\chi \in C^\infty_0(\mathbb R^{d+1})$ is not necessary in Theorem \ref{thCS}. In particular, when $q=r=2$, the function $\chi(t,x)=(1+|x|)^{-s}$, for $s>1/2$ is sufficient, see e.g. \cite{vega}. A close look at the proof of Theorem \ref{thCS} shows that in the general case where $r\geq 2$, $r>q$, the previous function is also sufficient. We will use that observation in the proof of our main result.
nodes.statement_short: The cut-off $\chi\in C_0^\infty$ in Theorem 2.1 can be replaced by $(1+|x|)^{-s}$, $s>1/2$, also when $r\ge2$, $r>q$.
nodes.label: remchi

nodes.name: Local smoothing for the local densities of the Liouville equation
nodes.statement: Let $n_{\sigma_\beta}$ and $n_{\gamma_\beta}$ be the local densities defined formally in {\rm (\ref{defn})} with $u_0 \in \mathcal J_p$ and $\varrho \in L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_p)$ for $p \in [1,\frac{2d}{2d-1})$. Then, $n_{\sigma_\beta}$ and $n_{\gamma_\beta}$ belong to $L^{r/2}(\mathbb R^{d+1})$, and we have the estimates \begin{equation} \|n_{\sigma_\beta}\|_{L^{r/2}(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \leq C_\chi \|u_0\|_{\mathcal J_p}, \qquad \|n_{\gamma_\beta}\|_{L^{r/2}(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \leq C_\chi \|\varrho\|_{L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_p)}, \end{equation} for $r \in [2,\infty)$ and $\beta >0$ such that $$ \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \displaystyle \displaystyle \beta < \frac{1+d}{r}-\frac{d}{2}, \qquad \textrm{if} \qquad p=1 \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad r>2\\[2mm] \displaystyle \beta \leq \frac{1}{2}, \qquad \textrm{if} \qquad p=1 \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad r=2\\[2mm] \displaystyle \beta < \frac{1+d}{r}-\frac{d}{2}-\frac{d}{p'}, \qquad \textrm{if} \qquad p>1. \end{array} \right. $$ Moreover, under the same conditions as above with $r=2$, we have the following estimates on the operators $\sigma_\beta$ and $\gamma_\beta$ defined in {\rm (\ref{defop})}: \begin{equation} \|\sigma_\beta\|_{L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_1)} \leq C_\chi \|u_0\|_{\mathcal J_p}, \qquad \|\gamma_\beta\|_{L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_1)} \leq C_\chi \|\varrho\|_{L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_p)}. \end{equation} The constant $C_\chi$ in {\rm (\ref{estnth})}-{\rm (\ref{esttraceth})} depends on $\chi$ but not on $u_0$ and $\varrho$.
nodes.statement_short: For data in $\mathcal J_p$, $p<2d/(2d-1)$, the localized densities $n_{\sigma_\beta},n_{\gamma_\beta}$ lie in $L^{r/2}$, and $\sigma_\beta,\gamma_\beta$ are trace class for $r=2$, for explicit ranges of $\beta$.

under the same conditions as above with $r=2$
conclusions: we have the following estimates on the operators $\sigma_\beta$ and $\gamma_\beta$ defined in {\rm (\ref{defop})}
The constant $C_\chi$ in {\rm (\ref{estnth})}-{\rm (\ref{esttraceth})} depends on $\chi$ but not on $u_0$ and $\varrho$.

nodes.name: Conditions for a positive smoothing exponent
nodes.statement: Note that for $\beta$ to be positive, the following conditions need to be satisfied: $$ r\leq 2+\frac{2}{d}, \qquad p <\frac{2d}{2d-1}, \qquad \frac{1}{p'}<\frac{1+d}{rd}-\frac{1}{2}. $$
nodes.statement_short: $\beta>0$ in Theorem 2.4 requires $r\le 2+2/d$, $p<2d/(2d-1)$ and $1/p'<(1+d)/(rd)-1/2$.

nodes.name: Optimality of Theorem 2.4
nodes.statement: Whether Theorem \ref{th1} is optimal or not is an open question.

nodes.name: Local fractional derivatives of the local densities n_Upsilon and n_Gamma
nodes.statement: Let $u_0 \in \mathcal J_p$ and $\varrho \in L^1(\mathbb R, \mathcal J_p)$ for $p \in [1,\frac{2d}{2d-1})$ and $\beta > 0$ such that $$ \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \displaystyle \beta \leq \frac{1}{2}, \qquad \textrm{if} \qquad p=1\\[2mm] \displaystyle \beta < \frac{1}{2}-\frac{d}{p'}, \qquad \textrm{if} \qquad p>1. \end{array} \right. $$ Then, for any $T>0$, any $v \in C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ and $\chi=|v|^2$, $D^\beta(\chi n_{\Upsilon})$ and $D^\beta(\chi n_{\Gamma})$ belong to $L^1(-T,T,L^{\frac{d}{d-\beta}}(\mathbb R^d))$, with the following estimates, $$ \| D^\beta(\chi n_{\Upsilon}) \|_{L^1(-T,T,L^{\frac{d}{d-\beta}}(\mathbb R^d))} \leq C_T \|u_0\|_{\mathcal J_p}, \quad \| D^\beta(\chi n_{\Gamma})\|_{L^1(-T,T,L^{\frac{d}{d-\beta}}(\mathbb R^d))} \leq C_T \|\varrho\|_{L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_p)}. $$ The constant $C_T$ above depends on $T$ and $v$ but not on $u_0$ and $\varrho$.
nodes.statement_short: For data in $\mathcal J_p$, $D^\beta(\chi n_\Upsilon)$ and $D^\beta(\chi n_\Gamma)$ lie in $L^1_tL^{d/(d-\beta)}_x$ locally, with explicit $\beta$.
assumptions: $u_0 \in \mathcal J_p$ and $\varrho \in L^1(\mathbb R, \mathcal J_p)$ for $p \in [1,\frac{2d}{2d-1})$ and $\beta > 0$ such that

The constant $C_T$ above depends on $T$ and $v$ but not on $u_0$ and $\varrho$.
also_stated_at: When $u_0$ and $\varrho$ are in some Schatten spaces of order $p\geq 1$, we show that the local density $n_u$ admits locally spatial fractional derivatives of order $\beta$, where $\beta$ depends on the dimension $d$ and $p$.
nodes.label: cor1

nodes.name: Only L^1 integrability in time in Corollary 2.5
nodes.statement: In Corollary \ref{cor1}, we only have an $L^1$ integrability in time since Theorem \ref{th1} was only exploited in the case $r=2$. The reason for this is explained in the proof of the corollary.
nodes.label: intime

nodes.name: Weighted extension of the Constantin-Saut estimate
nodes.statement: Let $\phi_t \equiv \phi(t,x) \in \mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d+1})$ and $\chi_t \equiv \chi(t,x) \in C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})$. Then, we have the following estimate: $$ \left\| (|x|^\alpha+1) \Lambda_{\alpha+\beta} \int_{\mathbb R } dt \, e^{-i t \Delta} \left(\chi_t \phi_t\right) \right\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)} \leq C_\chi \| \phi_t \|_{L^{r'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})}, $$ for $\alpha \in (0,\frac{1}{4}]$, $\beta \geq 0$, and $ r \in [2,\infty)$, such that \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{array}{l} \displaystyle 2\alpha+\beta < \frac{(d+1)}{r}-\frac{d}{2}, \qquad \textrm{if} \qquad r\in (2,\infty),\\ \displaystyle 2\alpha+\beta \leq \frac{1}{2}, \qquad \textrm{if} \qquad r =2. \end{array} \right. \end{equation} Moreover, the constant $C_\chi$ above depends on $\chi$ but not on $\phi$.
nodes.statement_short: Weighted version of Theorem 2.1: $\|(|x|^\alpha+1)\Lambda_{\alpha+\beta}\int e^{-it\Delta}\chi\phi\,dt\|_{L^2}\le C\|\phi\|_{L^{r'}}$ when $2\alpha+\beta$ is small.
assumptions: Let $\phi_t \equiv \phi(t,x) \in \mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d+1})$ and $\chi_t \equiv \chi(t,x) \in C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})$.
conclusions: Moreover, the constant $C_\chi$ above depends on $\chi$ but not on $\phi$.
nodes.label: pr1

nodes.name: Link between Lemma 2.7 and Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: In order to see the link with Theorem \ref{thCS}, note that $$ \mathcal F(\chi_t \varphi_t)(-|\xi|^2,\xi) = \mathcal F_x \left(\int_{\mathbb R } dt e^{-i t \Delta} \left(\chi_t \phi_t\right) \right)(\xi). $$

nodes.name: Heuristic proof idea of Lemma 2.7
nodes.statement: The result of Lemma \ref{pr1} is fairly intuitive: for the sake of simplicity, replace $|x|^\alpha$ by $x_1$ (the first coordinate of $x$); then, up to a commutator between $x_1$ and $\Lambda_{\alpha+\beta}$, we use the classical fact that $$ \Lambda_{\alpha+\beta} \, x_1\, e^{-it\Delta} = \Lambda_{\alpha+\beta}\, e^{-it\Delta} \, x_1+ 2 i t\Lambda_{\alpha+\beta}\, \partial_{x_1} \, e^{-it\Delta}. $$ The weights $x_1$ and $t $ in both terms of the r.h.s are handled by the fact that $\chi_t$ has a compact support, and the second term exhibits a loss of a derivative of order one (of order $\alpha$ in the Lemma, which explains {\rm (\ref{conslem})}). Of course, what makes Lemma \ref{pr1} non trivial is the fact that $\alpha$ is not an integer, which necessitates then the use of fractional derivatives for which there are no simple product and chain rules. In particular, the fractional derivatives are not local, which makes the use of Theorem \ref{thCS} not direct.
nodes.statement_short: Proof idea: replace $|x|^\alpha$ by $x_1$ and commute with $e^{-it\Delta}$, gaining a factor $t\partial_{x_1}$; compact support of $\chi$ handles the weights.

nodes.name: Dual version of Lemma 2.7
nodes.statement: The dual version of Lemma \ref{pr1} reads, under the same assumptions on the parameters, $$ \left(\int_{\mathbb R^{d+1}} |\chi(t,x)|^r | \Lambda_{\alpha+\beta} e^{it \Delta}\left((|\cdot|^\alpha+1)\varphi\right)(x) |^r dtdx \right)^{1/r} \leq C_\chi \|\varphi\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d})}. $$
nodes.label: dual2

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.4
nodes.statement:
The proof is an application of Theorem ef{thCS} and Lemma ef{pr1}. We focus on the term $\gamma_ eta$ and explain at the end of the proof the straighforward adaptation to $\sigma_ eta$. We remark first that we can limit ourselves to nonnegative operators $\varrho$ in $\mathcal J_p$, $p<\infty$. We can indeed decompose $\varrho$ as $\varrho=\varrho_+-\varrho_-$, $\varrho_{\pm} \geq 0$, $\varrho_+ \varrho_-=\varrho_- \varrho_+=0$, and the linearity of the trace yields $$ |n_{\gamma_ eta}|=|n_{\gamma_{+, eta}}-n_{\gamma_{-, eta}}| \leq n_{\gamma_{+, eta}}+n_{\gamma_{-, eta}}. $$ It suffices then to apply the estimates that we will derive for $n_{\gamma_{\pm, eta}}$, together with $$ \| \varrho_{\pm} \|_{\mathcal J_p} \leq \|\varrho\|_{\mathcal J_p}, \qquad p \in [1,\infty). $$ Also, in order to justify some formal computations, we consider ``smooth'' operators $\varrho$ satisfying the following conditions: $\varrho$ is finite rank and  egin{equation} \int_{\mathbb R} dt\, 	extrm{Tr} \Big((1+|x|^k) (-\Delta)^n \,\varrho(t)\, (-\Delta)^n (1+|x|^k)\Big) <\infty, \quad  orall k,n \in \mathbb N. \end{equation} The final estimates are then obtained by density since such operators are dense in $L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_p)$, $p<\infty$: on the one hand finite rank operators are dense in $\mathcal J_p$, $p<\infty$, and on the other, we have, for any smooth cut-off $\chi_\eta$ with $\chi_\eta(x) 	o 1$ pointwise as $\eta 	o 0$, $$ \chi_\eta e^{\eta \Delta}\, \varrho \, e^{\eta \Delta} \chi_\eta 	o \varrho \qquad 	extrm{in} \quad L^1(\mathbb R_+,\mathcal J_p) \qquad 	extrm{as} \qquad \eta 	o 0, $$ whenever $\varrho \in L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_p)$, $p\in [1,\infty]$. The regularity of $\varrho$ is then propagated to the operator $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^t e^{i (t-s) \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{-i (t-s) \Delta} ds$, see e.g. \cite{cazenave}, section 2.5, and as a consequence $\Gamma$ verifies $$ \sup_{t \in \mathbb R} 	extrm{Tr} \Big((1+|x|^k) (-\Delta)^n \,\Gamma(t)\, (-\Delta)^n (1+|x|^k)\Big) <\infty, \quad  orall k,n \in \mathbb N. $$ In particular, if $(\mu_j,\phi_j)_{j\in \mathbb N}$ is the spectral decomposition of $\Gamma$, this shows that $$ \sup_{t \in \mathbb R} \sum_{j \in \mathbb N} \mu_j(t) \left\|(1+|x|^k) (-\Delta)^n \,\phi_j(t)ight\|^2_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)} < \infty, \quad  orall k,n \in \mathbb N, $$ and therefore $(\mu_j(t))^{1/2}\phi_j(t) \in \mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ for all $t \in \mathbb R$.\ The proof starts with the following lemma:  egin{lemma} Let $ eta \in [0,1/2]$. For any $\varphi\in C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})$, the following relation holds: $$ \int_{\mathbb R} \int_{\mathbb R^d} dt dx\, n_{\gamma_ eta}(t,x) \varphi(t,x) =\int_{\mathbb R} ds 	extrm{Tr} \,  ig( e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{is \Delta} F_ eta(s)  ig), $$ where $$ F_ eta(s)=\int_{|s|}^\infty dt \, \Lambda_{ eta}e^{-i t \Delta }f_t e^{i t \Delta } \Lambda_{ eta} \in C^0(\mathbb R,\mathcal L(L^2(\mathbb R^d))), \qquad f_t=\chi_t \varphi_t \chi_t. $$ \end{lemma}  egin{proof} We begin with the following equalities, supposing that the support in $t$ of $\chi_t$ is included on $[-T,T]$:  egin{eqnarray*} \int_{\mathbb R} \int_{\mathbb R^d} dt dx \, n_{\gamma_ eta(t)}(t,x) \varphi(t,x) &=& \int_{-T}^T dt \, 	extrm{Tr}  ig( \gamma_ eta(t) \varphi_t  ig)\ &=&\int_{-T}^T dt \,	extrm{Tr} \left( \chi_t \Lambda_{ eta} \int_0^t ds e^{i(t- s) \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{-i (t-s) \Delta }\Lambda_{ eta} \chi_t \, \varphi_t ds ight)\ &=&\int_{-T}^T \int_0^t ds dt \, 	extrm{Tr} \Big( \chi_t \Lambda_{ eta}e^{i(t- s) \Delta} \varrho(s)e^{-i (t-s) \Delta }\Lambda_{ eta}\chi_t \, \varphi_t \Big)\[2mm] &:=&I. \end{eqnarray*} The last equality is justified by  egin{align} &\int_0^t ds \,\left|	extrm{Tr} \left( \chi_t \Lambda_{ eta}e^{i(t- s) \Delta} \varrho(s)e^{-i (t-s) \Delta }\Lambda_{ eta}\chi_t \, \varphi_t ight)ight| \ 
onumber &\hspace{2cm}=\int_0^t ds \,\left|	extrm{Tr} \left( \chi_t e^{i(t- s) \Delta} \Lambda_{ eta} \varrho(s)\Lambda_{ eta} e^{-i (t-s) \Delta }\chi_t \, \varphi_t ight)ight| \ 
onumber &\hspace{2cm} \leq \|\chi_t\|^2_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \|\varphi_t \|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \int_{\mathbb R} ds\, \| \Lambda_{ eta} \varrho(s) \Lambda_{ eta} \|_{\mathcal J_1} < \infty. \end{align} Above, we used the fact that $\Lambda_ eta$ and $e^{it \Delta}$ commute. Since the operator $\Lambda_ eta$ is not bounded, we need an additional step to justify the use of the cyclicity of the trace and to obtain that $$ I=\int_{-T}^T ds\,	extrm{Tr} \left( e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s)e^{i s \Delta } \Lambda_{ eta} \int_{|s|}^\infty dt e^{-i t \Delta} f_t e^{i t \Delta} \Lambda_{ eta} ight), $$ which would end the proof. We therefore regularize $I$ as $$ I_\eta=\int_{-T}^T \int_0^tds dt\, 	extrm{Tr} \left( \chi_t \Lambda^\eta \Lambda_{ eta} e^{i(t- s) \Delta} \varrho(s)e^{-i (t-s) \Delta }\Lambda_{ eta} \Lambda^\eta \chi_t \, \varphi_t ight), $$ where $\Lambda^\eta=(\mathbb{I}-\eta \Delta)^{-1}$. Similar estimates as in {m (ef{justi})} show that $I_\eta 	o I$ as $\eta 	o 0$. Using the semigroup property of $e^{it \Delta}$, and the fact that $\Lambda^\eta \Lambda_ eta$ is bounded, we can write  egin{eqnarray*} I_\eta &=&\int_{-T}^T \int_0^t ds dt\, 	extrm{Tr} \left(e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{is \Delta } e^{-i t \Delta}\Lambda_{ eta} \Lambda^\eta f_t \Lambda^\eta \Lambda_{ eta} e^{i t \Delta}ight) \ &=&\int_{-T}^T ds \int_{|s|}^\infty dt \,	extrm{Tr} \left(e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{is \Delta } \Lambda_{ eta} \Lambda^\eta e^{-i t \Delta} f_t e^{i t \Delta} \Lambda^\eta \Lambda_{ eta} ight)\ &=&\int_{-T}^T ds\, 	extrm{Tr}  ig( e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{is \Delta} F^\eta_ eta(s)  ig), \end{eqnarray*} where, for all $s\in \mathbb R$, $$ F^\eta_ eta(s):=\int_{|s|}^\infty dt \Lambda_{ eta}\Lambda^\eta e^{-i t \Delta }f_t e^{i t \Delta } \Lambda^\eta \Lambda_{ eta}\in \mathcal L(L^2(\mathbb R^d)). $$ Above, the use of the Fubini theorem and the inversion of the integral and the trace are justified by similar estimates as {m (ef{justi})}. We now show that $F^\eta_ eta 	o F_ eta$ in $C^0([-T,T],\mathcal L(L^2(\mathbb R^d)))$ as $\eta 	o 0$. We remark first that $F_ eta(s) \in \mathcal L(L^2(\mathbb R^d))$ for all $s \in [-T,T]$ and $ eta \in [0,1/2]$ thanks to Theorem ef{thCS} and Remark ef{remdual}. Indeed, for any $v \in C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$,  egin{eqnarray*} \| F_ eta(s) v \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}&=&\left\| \Lambda_{ eta} \int_{\mathbb R} dt e^{-i t \Delta } \chi_t g_t ight\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}, \qquad g_t:={\mathbbmss{1}}_{(|s|,\infty)} \varphi_t \chi_t \Lambda_{ eta} e^{i t \Delta } v,\ &\leq & C \|g_t \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^{d+1})}\ & \leq & C \|\varphi_t\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \|\chi_t \Lambda_{ eta} e^{i t \Delta } v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^{d+1})}\ &\leq & C \|v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}. \end{eqnarray*} The continuity of $F_ eta(s)$ in $s$ is straightforward. We then write $$ F_ eta^\eta-F_ eta=(\Lambda^\eta-\mathbb{I}) F_ eta \Lambda^\eta+F_ eta (\Lambda^\eta-\mathbb{I}), $$ and conclude with the fact that $(\Lambda^\eta-\mathbb{I})	o 0$ in $\mathcal L(L^2(\mathbb R^{d}))$ together with $F_ eta \in C^0([-T,T],\mathcal L(L^2(\mathbb R^d)))$. This ends the proof of the lemma since $F_ eta(s)=0$ for $|s| \geq T$. \end{proof} \paragraph{The case $\varrho$ trace class.} From Lemma ef{expdens}, we have  egin{eqnarray*} \left|\int_{\mathbb R} \int_{\mathbb R^d} n_{\gamma_ eta}(t,x) \varphi(t,x) dt dx ight| &\leq& \sup_{s \in \mathbb R} \| F_ eta(s) \| \int_{\mathbb R} ds \, 	extrm{Tr}  ig( e^{i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{- is \Delta}  ig)\ &=&\sup_{s \in \mathbb R} \| F_ eta(s) \| \|\varrho\|_{L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_1)}, \end{eqnarray*} and it remains to estimate $F_ eta$ in terms of $\varphi$. As in the proof of Lemma ef{expdens}, we write  egin{eqnarray*} \| F_ eta(s) v \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}&=&\left\| \Lambda_{ eta} \int_{\mathbb R} dt e^{-i t \Delta } \chi_t g_t ight\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}, \qquad g_t={\mathbbmss{1}}_{(|s|,\infty)} \varphi_t \chi_t \Lambda_{ eta} e^{i t \Delta } v,\ &\leq & C \|g_t \|_{L^{r'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})}\ & \leq & C \|\varphi_t\|_{L^{r'q'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \|\chi_t \Lambda_{ eta} e^{i t \Delta } v\|_{L^{r'q}(\mathbb R^{d+1})}\ &\leq & C \|\varphi_t\|_{L^{r'q'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \|v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}. \end{eqnarray*} The first inequality above is an application of Theorem ef{thCS} with parameters satisfying  egin{equation} \left\{ egin{array}{l} \displaystyle  eta <  rac{1+d}{r}- rac{d}{2} \qquad 	extrm{if} \qquad 1 \leq r' <2, \qquad \ \displaystyle  eta\leq  rac{1}{2} \qquad 	extrm{if} \qquad r'=2. \end{array} ight. \end{equation} The second inequality follows from the H"older inequality with $1\leq q \leq \infty$, and the last inequality is a consequence of the dual version of Theorem ef{thCS} given in Remark ef{remdual}, provided we have the relations  egin{equation} \left\{ egin{array}{l} \displaystyle  eta <  rac{1+d}{r' q}- rac{d}{2} \qquad 	extrm{if} \qquad 2< r'q <\infty, \qquad \ \displaystyle  eta\leq  rac{1}{2} \qquad 	extrm{if} \qquad r'q=2. \end{array} ight. \end{equation} We optimize the right-hand-side of the inequalities of {m (ef{eqq1})}-{m (ef{eqq2})} by setting $q=1$ when $r'=2$, and when $r'<2$, we set $r'q=r$, i.e. $q=r-1$. In this case, $r'q'=r/(r-2)$ and $r'q'/(r'q'-1)=r/2$, which yields by duality the estimate $$ \|n_{\gamma_ eta}\|_{L^{r/2}(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \leq C \|\varrho\|_{L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_1)}, \qquad 	extrm{with} \qquad \left\{ egin{array}{l} \displaystyle  eta <  rac{1+d}{r}- rac{d}{2} \qquad 	extrm{if} \qquad 1\leq r'<2, \qquad \ \displaystyle  eta\leq  rac{1}{2} \qquad 	extrm{if} \qquad r'=2. \end{array} ight. $$ Note that for $ eta$ to be positive, we need the condition $r < 2(d+1)/d$. \paragraph{The case $\varrho \in \mathcal J_p$, $p>1$.} This case is more interesting since new estimates are required. We start as before with Lemma ef{expdens}. Since $\varrho$ is not trace class, one may expect a lower value for the exponent $ eta$. A simple way to proceed is to compensate for the fact that $\varrho 
otin \mathcal J_1$ by introducing the operator $J_\alpha:=\Lambda_\alpha (1+|x|^\alpha)$ for an appropriate $\alpha$ in  egin{eqnarray*} 	extrm{Tr} \,  ig( e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{is \Delta} F_ eta(s)  ig)&=&	extrm{Tr} \, \left( J_\alpha J_\alpha^{-1} e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{is \Delta} (J_\alpha^*)^{-1}J_\alpha^* F_ eta(s) ight):=II(s). \end{eqnarray*} As in the proof of Lemma ef{expdens}, we cannot use directly the cyclicity of the trace since $J_\alpha$ is not bounded. We therefore introduce a regularization as before, with the difference that we now use Lemma ef{pr1} instead of Theorem ef{thCS} to pass to the limit. This justifies the fact that  egin{eqnarray} 
onumber |II(s)|&=&\left|	extrm{Tr} \, \left( J_\alpha^{-1} e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{is \Delta} (J_\alpha^*)^{-1}J_\alpha^* F_ eta(s) J_\alpha ight) ight|\ &\leq & 	extrm{Tr} \, \left( J_\alpha^{-1} e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{is \Delta} (J_\alpha^*)^{-1} ight) \| J_\alpha^* F_ eta(s) J_\alpha \|. \end{eqnarray} Using the H"older inequality for $\mathcal J_p$ spaces, we find $$ 	extrm{Tr} \, \left( J_\alpha^{-1} e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{is \Delta} (J_\alpha^*)^{-1} ight) \leq \|\varrho(s)\|_{\mathcal J_p} \| J_\alpha^{-1} \|^2_{\mathcal J_{2p'}} = \|\varrho(s)\|_{\mathcal J_p} \| (1+|x|^\alpha)^{-1} \Lambda_{-\alpha}\|^2_{\mathcal J_{2p'}}. $$ Above, we used the facts that $(J_\alpha^*)^{-1}=(J_\alpha^{-1})^{*}$ and that the $\mathcal J_p$ norms of $A$ and $A^*$ are equal. The Kato-Seiler-Simon inequality \cite{Simon-trace}, Chapter 4, then yields $$ \| (1+|x|^\alpha)^{-1} \Lambda_{-\alpha}\|_{\mathcal J_{2p'}} \leq C \|(1+|x|^\alpha)^{-1}\|_{L^{2p'}(\mathbb R^d)} \|(1+|x|^2)^{-\alpha/2}\|_{L^{2p'}(\mathbb R^d)}, $$ which is finite whenever $2\alpha p'>d$. It remains to treat the term in {m (ef{T2})} involving $F_ eta$. It is treated in the same fashion as in case $p=1$, with the difference that we use Lemma ef{pr1} and its dual version instead of Theorem ef{thCS}. Hence, with $$ g_t={\mathbbmss{1}}_{(|s|,\infty)} \varphi_t \chi_t \Lambda_{\alpha+ eta} e^{i t \Delta } (1+|x|^\alpha) v, $$ we find the estimate  egin{eqnarray*} \| J_\alpha^* F_ eta(s) J_\alpha v \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}&=&\left\| (1+|x|^\alpha)\Lambda_{\alpha+ eta} \int_{\mathbb R} dt e^{-i t \Delta } \chi_t g_t ight\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}\ &\leq & C \|\varphi_t\|_{L^{r'q'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \|v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}, \end{eqnarray*} under the conditions $$ 2\alpha+ eta <  rac{1+d}{r}- rac{d}{2}, \qquad 	extrm{for} \qquad1 < r' < 2, \qquad 	extrm{and} \qquad 2\alpha+ eta \leq  rac{1}{2}, \qquad 	extrm{for} \qquad r'=2. $$ Owing to $2\alpha p'>d$, the latter condition becomes the one of Theorem ef{th1}. Going back to Lemma ef{expdens}, this finally yields by duality $$ \|n_{\gamma_ eta}\|_{L^{r/2}(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \leq C \|\varrho\|_{L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_p)}, \qquad 1 < r' \leq 2, \qquad  eta <  rac{1+d}{r}- rac{d}{2}- rac{d}{p'}. $$ Note that for $ eta$ to be positive, we need the conditions $$ r\leq 2+ rac{2}{d}, \qquad p'>2d, \qquad  rac{1}{p'}< rac{d+1}{rd}- rac{1}{2}. $$  egin{remark} It is interesting to explore another route to the above estimate on $n_{\gamma_ eta}$. Instead of introducing the operators $J_\alpha$, the term $II$ could be directly bounded by $$ \|\varrho\|_{\mathcal J_p} \|F_ eta(s)\|_{\mathcal J_{p'}}, \qquad p>1. $$ The main difficulty is now to estimate $F_ eta$ in the Schatten space $\mathcal J_{p'}$. This does not seem direct, in particular it is unclear whether the method of \cite{LewStri}, which is used to derive Strichartz estimates and consists in writing $	extrm{Tr}((F_ eta)^{p'})$ (when $p'$ is an integer) as a multiple integral in time and in switching trace and integration, can be employed or not since the order of integration matters for estimating $F_ eta$. \end{remark} \paragraph{Estimates {m (ef{esttraceth})} and conclusion.} We address now estimates {m (ef{esttraceth})}, which are direct according to what was previously done: adapting Lemma ef{expdens} yields $$ \|\gamma_ eta\|_{L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_1)} = \int_{\mathbb R} dt\, 	extrm{Tr}  ig( \gamma_ eta(t) ig)= \int_{\mathbb R} dt\, 	extrm{Tr}  ig( \varrho(t) F_ eta(t)  ig), $$ where $F_ eta$ is the same as in Lemma ef{expdens} with now $\varphi_t\equiv 1$. Introducing the operator $J_\alpha$ as before, we find $$ \|\gamma_ eta\|_{L^1(\mathbb R_+,\mathcal J_1)} \leq C \sup_{t\in \mathbb R} \| J_\alpha^* F_ eta(t) J_\alpha\| \int_{\mathbb R} dt\, \| \varrho(t)\|_{\mathcal J_p}, $$ and we already know that the term involving $F_ eta$ is finite provided $ eta$ satisfies the conditions of Theorem ef{th1} with $r=2$. A similar method yields the estimate on $\sigma_ eta$. This concludes the proof of the estimates involving $\gamma_ eta$. The estimates on $n_{\sigma_ eta}$ are derived with the relation $$ \int_{\mathbb R} \int_{\mathbb R^d} n_{\sigma_ eta}(t,x) \varphi(t,x) dt dx = 	extrm{Tr}  ig( u_0 F_ eta(0)  ig), $$ and estimating $F_ eta$ as before. This ends the proof of Theorem ef{th1}.
nodes.statement_short: Duality: express $\int n_{\gamma_\beta}\varphi$ as a trace against $F_\beta$ (Lemma 3.1) and bound $F_\beta$ via Theorem 2.1 or Lemma 2.7. For $p>1$ the weight $J_\alpha=\Lambda_\alpha(1+|x|^\alpha)$ with Kato-Seiler-Simon compensates for non-trace-class data.

nodes.name: Trace representation of the local density pairing
nodes.statement: Let $\beta \in [0,1/2]$. For any $\varphi\in C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})$, the following relation holds: $$ \int_{\mathbb R} \int_{\mathbb R^d} dt dx\, n_{\gamma_\beta}(t,x) \varphi(t,x) =\int_{\mathbb R} ds \textrm{Tr} \, \big( e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{is \Delta} F_\beta(s) \big), $$ where $$ F_\beta(s)=\int_{|s|}^\infty dt \, \Lambda_{\beta}e^{-i t \Delta }f_t e^{i t \Delta } \Lambda_{\beta} \in C^0(\mathbb R,\mathcal L(L^2(\mathbb R^d))), \qquad f_t=\chi_t \varphi_t \chi_t. $$
nodes.statement_short: $\int n_{\gamma_\beta}\varphi=\int \mathrm{Tr}(e^{-is\Delta}\varrho(s)e^{is\Delta}F_\beta(s))ds$ with $F_\beta$ a bounded-operator-valued integral.
conclusions: the following relation holds: $$ \int_{\mathbb R} \int_{\mathbb R^d} dt dx\, n_{\gamma_\beta}(t,x) \varphi(t,x) =\int_{\mathbb R} ds \textrm{Tr} \, \big( e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{is \Delta} F_\beta(s) \big), $$ where $$ F_\beta(s)=\int_{|s|}^\infty dt \, \Lambda_{\beta}e^{-i t \Delta }f_t e^{i t \Delta } \Lambda_{\beta} \in C^0(\mathbb R,\mathcal L(L^2(\mathbb R^d))), \qquad f_t=\chi_t \varphi_t \chi_t. $$
nodes.label: expdens

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: We begin with the following equalities, supposing that the support in $t$ of $\chi_t$ is included on $[-T,T]$: \begin{eqnarray*} \int_{\mathbb R} \int_{\mathbb R^d} dt dx \, n_{\gamma_\beta(t)}(t,x) \varphi(t,x) &=& \int_{-T}^T dt \, \textrm{Tr} \big( \gamma_\beta(t) \varphi_t \big)\\ &=&\int_{-T}^T dt \,\textrm{Tr} \left( \chi_t \Lambda_{\beta} \int_0^t ds e^{i(t- s) \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{-i (t-s) \Delta }\Lambda_{\beta} \chi_t \, \varphi_t ds \right)\\ &=&\int_{-T}^T \int_0^t ds dt \, \textrm{Tr} \Big( \chi_t \Lambda_{\beta}e^{i(t- s) \Delta} \varrho(s)e^{-i (t-s) \Delta }\Lambda_{\beta}\chi_t \, \varphi_t \Big)\\[2mm] &:=&I. \end{eqnarray*} The last equality is justified by \begin{align} &\int_0^t ds \,\left|\textrm{Tr} \left( \chi_t \Lambda_{\beta}e^{i(t- s) \Delta} \varrho(s)e^{-i (t-s) \Delta }\Lambda_{\beta}\chi_t \, \varphi_t \right)\right| \\ \nonumber &\hspace{2cm}=\int_0^t ds \,\left|\textrm{Tr} \left( \chi_t e^{i(t- s) \Delta} \Lambda_{\beta} \varrho(s)\Lambda_{\beta} e^{-i (t-s) \Delta }\chi_t \, \varphi_t \right)\right| \\ \nonumber &\hspace{2cm} \leq \|\chi_t\|^2_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \|\varphi_t \|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \int_{\mathbb R} ds\, \| \Lambda_{\beta} \varrho(s) \Lambda_{\beta} \|_{\mathcal J_1} < \infty. \end{align} Above, we used the fact that $\Lambda_\beta$ and $e^{it \Delta}$ commute. Since the operator $\Lambda_\beta$ is not bounded, we need an additional step to justify the use of the cyclicity of the trace and to obtain that $$ I=\int_{-T}^T ds\,\textrm{Tr} \left( e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s)e^{i s \Delta } \Lambda_{\beta} \int_{|s|}^\infty dt e^{-i t \Delta} f_t e^{i t \Delta} \Lambda_{\beta} \right), $$ which would end the proof. We therefore regularize $I$ as $$ I_\eta=\int_{-T}^T \int_0^tds dt\, \textrm{Tr} \left( \chi_t \Lambda^\eta \Lambda_{\beta} e^{i(t- s) \Delta} \varrho(s)e^{-i (t-s) \Delta }\Lambda_{\beta} \Lambda^\eta \chi_t \, \varphi_t \right), $$ where $\Lambda^\eta=(\mathbb{I}-\eta \Delta)^{-1}$. Similar estimates as in {\rm (\ref{justi})} show that $I_\eta \to I$ as $\eta \to 0$. Using the semigroup property of $e^{it \Delta}$, and the fact that $\Lambda^\eta \Lambda_\beta$ is bounded, we can write \begin{eqnarray*} I_\eta &=&\int_{-T}^T \int_0^t ds dt\, \textrm{Tr} \left(e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{is \Delta } e^{-i t \Delta}\Lambda_{\beta} \Lambda^\eta f_t \Lambda^\eta \Lambda_{\beta} e^{i t \Delta}\right) \\ &=&\int_{-T}^T ds \int_{|s|}^\infty dt \,\textrm{Tr} \left(e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{is \Delta } \Lambda_{\beta} \Lambda^\eta e^{-i t \Delta} f_t e^{i t \Delta} \Lambda^\eta \Lambda_{\beta} \right)\\ &=&\int_{-T}^T ds\, \textrm{Tr} \big( e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{is \Delta} F^\eta_\beta(s) \big), \end{eqnarray*} where, for all $s\in \mathbb R$, $$ F^\eta_\beta(s):=\int_{|s|}^\infty dt \Lambda_{\beta}\Lambda^\eta e^{-i t \Delta }f_t e^{i t \Delta } \Lambda^\eta \Lambda_{\beta}\in \mathcal L(L^2(\mathbb R^d)). $$ Above, the use of the Fubini theorem and the inversion of the integral and the trace are justified by similar estimates as {\rm (\ref{justi})}. We now show that $F^\eta_\beta \to F_\beta$ in $C^0([-T,T],\mathcal L(L^2(\mathbb R^d)))$ as $\eta \to 0$. We remark first that $F_\beta(s) \in \mathcal L(L^2(\mathbb R^d))$ for all $s \in [-T,T]$ and $\beta \in [0,1/2]$ thanks to Theorem \ref{thCS} and Remark \ref{remdual}. Indeed, for any $v \in C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, \begin{eqnarray*} \| F_\beta(s) v \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}&=&\left\| \Lambda_{\beta} \int_{\mathbb R} dt e^{-i t \Delta } \chi_t g_t \right\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}, \qquad g_t:={\mathbbmss{1}}_{(|s|,\infty)} \varphi_t \chi_t \Lambda_{\beta} e^{i t \Delta } v,\\ &\leq & C \|g_t \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^{d+1})}\\ & \leq & C \|\varphi_t\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \|\chi_t \Lambda_{\beta} e^{i t \Delta } v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^{d+1})}\\ &\leq & C \|v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}. \end{eqnarray*} The continuity of $F_\beta(s)$ in $s$ is straightforward. We then write $$ F_\beta^\eta-F_\beta=(\Lambda^\eta-\mathbb{I}) F_\beta \Lambda^\eta+F_\beta (\Lambda^\eta-\mathbb{I}), $$ and conclude with the fact that $(\Lambda^\eta-\mathbb{I})\to 0$ in $\mathcal L(L^2(\mathbb R^{d}))$ together with $F_\beta \in C^0([-T,T],\mathcal L(L^2(\mathbb R^d)))$. This ends the proof of the lemma since $F_\beta(s)=0$ for $|s| \geq T$.
nodes.statement_short: Fubini and cyclicity of the trace, justified by regularizing with $(I-\eta\Delta)^{-1}$ and passing to the limit using Theorem 2.1 and Remark 2.2.

nodes.name: Alternative route via Schatten bounds on F_beta
nodes.statement: It is interesting to explore another route to the above estimate on $n_{\gamma_\beta}$. Instead of introducing the operators $J_\alpha$, the term $II$ could be directly bounded by $$ \|\varrho\|_{\mathcal J_p} \|F_\beta(s)\|_{\mathcal J_{p'}}, \qquad p>1. $$ The main difficulty is now to estimate $F_\beta$ in the Schatten space $\mathcal J_{p'}$. This does not seem direct, in particular it is unclear whether the method of \cite{LewStri}, which is used to derive Strichartz estimates and consists in writing $\textrm{Tr}((F_\beta)^{p'})$ (when $p'$ is an integer) as a multiple integral in time and in switching trace and integration, can be employed or not since the order of integration matters for estimating $F_\beta$.
nodes.statement_short: Bounding $II$ directly by $\|\varrho\|_{\mathcal J_p}\|F_\beta\|_{\mathcal J_{p'}}$ would need Schatten estimates on $F_\beta$, which are unclear.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.7
nodes.statement: Let $u_t:=\chi_t \phi_t \in C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})$ and define $$ I:=(|x|^\alpha+1) \Lambda_{\alpha+\beta} \int_{\mathbb R } dt e^{-i t \Delta} u_t. $$ We then write, for $[A,B]=AB-BA$ the usual commutator between operators, \begin{eqnarray*} I&=&\Lambda_{\alpha+\beta} (|x|^\alpha+1) \int_{\mathbb R } dt e^{-i t \Delta} u_t+ \big[|x|^\alpha+1,\Lambda_{\alpha+\beta}\big] \int_{\mathbb R } dt e^{-i t \Delta} u_t\\ &:=&I_0+I_1+I_2, \end{eqnarray*} where $$ I_0=\Lambda_{\alpha+\beta} |x|^\alpha \int_{\mathbb R } dt e^{-i t \Delta} u_t, \qquad I_1=\Lambda_{\alpha+\beta} \int_{\mathbb R } dt e^{-i t \Delta} u_t, $$ and $I_2$ is the term involving the commutator. We start with $I_0$, the most singular term. \paragraph{The term $I_0$.} For $\varphi$ smooth and $\alpha>0$, let $$ A^\alpha_t \varphi(x):=2^\alpha t^\alpha e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4t}} D^\alpha \left( e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4t}} \varphi(x)\right). $$ Then, according to \cite{ponce}, Proposition 3, we have the following commutation relation between $|x|^\alpha$ and the operator $e^{-it \Delta}$: $$ |x|^\alpha e^{-i t \Delta} \varphi= e^{-i t \Delta} A^\alpha_t \varphi. $$ This leads to the decomposition of $I_0$ below: \begin{eqnarray*} I_0&=&2^\alpha \Lambda_{\alpha+\beta}\int_{\mathbb R } dt e^{-i t \Delta}\left[ t^\alpha e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4t}} D^\alpha \left( e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4t}} u_t \right) \right]\\ &:=&J_1+J_2, \end{eqnarray*} with \begin{align*} &J_1=2^\alpha \Lambda_{\alpha+\beta}\int_{\mathbb R } dt e^{-i t \Delta}D^\alpha \left( t^\alpha u_t \right)\\ &J_2=2^\alpha \Lambda_{\alpha+\beta}\int_{\mathbb R } dt \,t^\alpha e^{-i t \Delta}\left[ e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4t}} D^\alpha \left( e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4t}} u_t \right)-D^\alpha \left( u_t \right) \right]. \end{align*} The term $J_1$ is directly estimated with Theorem \ref{thCS}: since $D^\alpha$ and $e^{-it \Delta}$ commute, we have $$ \| J_1\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)} \leq C \left\| \Lambda_{2 \alpha+\beta}\int_{\mathbb R } dt e^{-i t \Delta} \, t^\alpha u_t \right\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}, $$ and therefore, applying Theorem \ref{thCS} with $q=2$, and supposing that the support of $\chi_t$ in the $t$ variable is included in $[-T,T]$, the following estimate holds \begin{equation} \| J_1\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)} \leq C \|t^\alpha \phi_t\|_{L^{r'}((-T,T)\times \mathbb R^{d})} \leq C \|\phi_t\|_{L^{r'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})}, \end{equation} with \begin{equation} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \displaystyle 2\alpha+\beta < \frac{(d+1)}{r}-\frac{d}{2}, \qquad r'\in [1,2).\\ \displaystyle 2\alpha+\beta \leq \frac{1}{2}, \qquad r'=2. \end{array} \right. \end{equation} This treats the leading term and yields the condition on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ stated in the lemma. We turn now to the term $J_2$. For $\varphi \in C^1_c(\mathbb R^{d})$, we use the following representation formula for the fractional Laplacian (see e.g. \cite{stein1}): we have, for any $\alpha \in (0,1)$, \begin{equation} D^\alpha(\varphi)(x)=c_{d,\alpha} \int_{\mathbb R^d} \frac{\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)}{|x-y|^{d+\alpha}} dy. \end{equation} Note that there is no need to introduce a principal value in the definition since $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and $\varphi \in C^1$. We then write \begin{eqnarray*} e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4t}} D^\alpha \left( e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4t}} t^\alpha u_t \right)-D^\alpha \left( t^\alpha u_t \right)&=&c_{d,\alpha} \int_{\mathbb R^d} \frac{t^\alpha u_t(x)- e^{i\frac{|x|^2-|y|^2}{4t}} t^\alpha u_t(y)}{|x-y|^{d+\alpha}} dy-D^\alpha \left( t^\alpha u_t \right)\\ &=&c_{d,\alpha} \int_{\mathbb R^d} \frac{(1- e^{i\frac{|x|^2-|y|^2}{4t}}) t^\alpha u_t(y)}{|x-y|^{d+\alpha}} dy\\[3mm] &:=&R_{t,0}. \end{eqnarray*} We need now to estimate a term of the form $$ \Lambda_{\alpha+\beta}\int_{\mathbb R } dt e^{-i t \Delta} R_{t,0}. $$ For this, we cannot directly apply Theorem \ref{thCS} since the function $R_{t,0}$ does not have the required regularity and compact support. This is therefore where we invoke Remark \ref{remchi} and the fact that the function $\chi(t,x)=(1+|x|)^{-s}$ for $s>1/2$ is sufficient. We actually choose $(1+|x|)^{-1}$ for simplicity. Then, \begin{eqnarray*} (1+|x|) R_{t,0} &=&c_{d,\alpha} \int_{\mathbb R^d} (1+|y|)\frac{(1- e^{i\frac{|x|^2-|y|^2}{4t}}) t^\alpha u_t(y)}{|x-y|^{d+\alpha}} dy\\ &&+c_{d,\alpha} \int_{\mathbb R^d} (|x|-|y|)\frac{(1- e^{i\frac{|x|^2-|y|^2}{4t}}) t^\alpha u_t(y)}{|x-y|^{d+\alpha}} dy\\ &:=&R_{t,1}+R_{t,2}. \end{eqnarray*} This yields $$ J_2=2^\alpha \Lambda_{\alpha+\beta}\int_{\mathbb R } dt e^{-i t \Delta}(1+|x|)^{-1}\left[R_{t,1}+R_{t,2}\right], $$ and as a consequence of Theorem \ref{thCS}, \begin{equation} \| J_2\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)} \leq C \|R_{t,1}+R_{t,2}\|_{L^{q'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})},\; \textrm{with} \; \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \displaystyle \alpha+\beta < \frac{(d+1)}{q}-\frac{d}{2}, \quad q'\in [1,2).\\ \displaystyle \alpha+\beta \leq \frac{1}{2}, \quad q'=2. \end{array} \right. \end{equation} We estimate now $R_{t,1}+R_{t,2}$. We will actually only treat the most singular term $R_{t,1}$ since $R_{t,2}$ follows from the same techniques. We will use for this the simple inequality below, for $a \in [0,1]$, \begin{equation} \left| 1- e^{i\frac{|x|^2-|y|^2}{4t}}\right| \leq 2^{1-3a}t^{-a} |x+y|^a|x-y|^a\leq 2^{1-3a}t^{-a}\left( 2^a|y|^a|x-y|^{a} +|x-y|^{2a}\right). \end{equation} Using {\rm (\ref{AF})} in $R_{t,1}$ with $a=\alpha+\varepsilon$, for some $\varepsilon>0$ such that $\varepsilon \leq 1-\alpha$, we find \begin{eqnarray*} |R_{t,1}| &\leq& C t^{-\varepsilon} \int_{\mathbb R^d} (1+|y|^{1+\alpha+\varepsilon})\frac{|u_t(y)|}{|x-y|^{d-\varepsilon}} dy+C t^{-\varepsilon} \int_{\mathbb R^d} (1+|y|)\frac{|u_t(y)|}{|x-y|^{d-\alpha-2\varepsilon}} dy\\ &:=&R_{t,3}+R_{t,4}. \end{eqnarray*} We start with the most singular term $R_{t,3}$. For any $r'\in (1,2]$ as in {\rm (\ref{estJ1})}, we claim that we can find $q'$ (the one in {\rm (\ref{estJ2})}) and $\varepsilon>0$ such that \begin{equation} \|R_{t,3}\|_{L^{q'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \leq C \|\phi_t\|_{L^{r'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})}. \end{equation} We will use for this the following classical estimate on Riesz potentials, see e.g. the Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality of \cite{RS-80-2}, section IX.4, \begin{equation} \left\| \int_{\mathbb R^d} \frac{\varphi(y)}{|\cdot-y|^{d-\varepsilon}} dy \right\|_{L^{\frac{s d}{d-\varepsilon s}}(\mathbb R^d)} \leq C \|\varphi\|_{L^s(\mathbb R^d)}, \qquad 1<s<\infty, \qquad 1<\frac{s d}{d-\varepsilon s}<\infty. \end{equation} Fix now $r'\in (1,2]$ as in {\rm (\ref{estJ1})}, and set $q'=\frac{s d}{d-\varepsilon s}$ in {\rm (\ref{estJ2})} for some $s$ such that $1<s<r'$. Then, for {\rm (\ref{estJ2})} (in the case $q'<2$) and {\rm (\ref{riesz})} to hold, it is required that \begin{equation} 1<\frac{s d}{d-\varepsilon s} < 2, \qquad \alpha+\beta < \left(\frac{1}{s'}+\frac{\varepsilon}{d}\right)(d+1)-\frac{d}{2}, \qquad r<s'<\infty. \end{equation} Using {\rm (\ref{riesz})} and the H\"older inequality, it follows that \begin{eqnarray} \nonumber \|R_{t,3}\|_{L^{q'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})} &\leq& C\| t^{-\varepsilon} (1+|x|^{1+\alpha+\varepsilon}) u_t \|_{L^{q'}(\mathbb R_t,L^{s}(\mathbb R_x^{d}))} \\\nonumber &\leq& C\| t^{-\varepsilon} u_t \|_{L^{q'}(\mathbb R_t,L^{r'}(\mathbb R_x^{d}))}\\ &\leq& C\left(\int_{-T}^T t^{-\varepsilon q' p' } \right)^{1/(q'p')} \|\phi_t\|_{L^{r'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})}, \end{eqnarray} where $pq'=r'$, $p\in (1,\infty)$. In the second line above, we used the fact that $u_t$ has a compact support in order to control the $L^s_x$ norm of $u_t$ by the $L^{r'}_x$ norm, which is possible since $s<r'$. With $pq'=r'$ and $q'=\frac{s d}{d-\varepsilon s}$, we find therefore $$ p'=r' \left(\frac{d-\varepsilon s }{r'(d-\varepsilon s)-sd}\right) $$ with the constraints \begin{equation} p=\frac{r'}{q'}=\frac{(d-\varepsilon s)r'}{sd} > 1, \qquad i.e. \qquad 1<s<\frac{dr'}{d+\varepsilon r'}. \end{equation} For the first term of {\rm (\ref{intT})} to be finite, we need $\varepsilon q'p'<1$, that is \begin{equation} \varepsilon q' p'=\frac{\varepsilon r'sd}{r'(d-\varepsilon s)-sd}<1, \qquad i.e. \qquad sr'\varepsilon (d+1)+sd<dr'. \end{equation} When the latter inequality is satisfied, it implies the second inequality in {\rm (\ref{eqp})} that we thus ignore. We collect now the various constraints on the parameters and define $\varepsilon$ and $s$ appropriately. The first inequality in {\rm (\ref{const})} becomes $$ \frac{1}{2} < \frac{1}{s}-\frac{\varepsilon}{d}<1. $$ The second inequality holds since $s>1$ and $\varepsilon>0$, and we therefore only keep the first one. Defining $\delta$ by $r'=s+\delta$, with $0<\delta<r'-1$ since $r'>s>1$, {\rm (\ref{est4})} and the above inequality become \begin{equation} r' (r'-\delta) \varepsilon (d+1)<\delta d, \qquad \frac{1}{2} < \frac{1}{r'-\delta}-\frac{\varepsilon}{d}. \end{equation} We have in addition $r'\in (1,2]$ as well as \begin{equation} 0<\varepsilon\leq 1-\alpha, \qquad \alpha+\beta < \left(\frac{1}{s'}+\frac{\varepsilon}{d}\right)(d+1)-\frac{d}{2}. \end{equation} Since $r'\leq 2$ and $\delta>0$, $r'-\delta \leq 2-\delta<2$, the inequalities in {\rm (\ref{const5})} are satisfied as soon as $$ 4 (d+1) \varepsilon \leq \delta d, \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \frac{1}{2} <\frac{1}{2-\delta}-\frac{\varepsilon}{d}, \qquad \textrm{that is for the latter} \qquad \frac{4\varepsilon}{d+2\varepsilon} < \delta. $$ These latter inequalities are satisfied for instance when $$ \varepsilon=\frac{\delta d}{4(d+1)} < \frac{1}{4} \qquad (\textrm{since} \quad\delta <r'-1\leq 1), $$ and we verify that $\alpha+\varepsilon \leq 1$ since $\alpha \leq 1/4$. It remains to choose $\delta$. We need to do it in such a way that $0<\delta<r'-1$ and such that the second inequality of {\rm (\ref{const3})} holds when {\rm (\ref{mainconst})} is verified. The latter condition can be expressed as the inequality, for $r \in [2,\infty)$, $$ \frac{(d+1)}{r}\leq \left(\frac{1}{s'}+\frac{\varepsilon}{d}\right)(d+1)+\alpha. $$ With direct algebra and our current choice of $\varepsilon$, this becomes \begin{equation} \frac{\delta}{r'(r'-\delta)} \leq \frac{\varepsilon}{d}+\frac{\alpha}{d+1}=\frac{\delta }{4(d+1)}+\frac{\alpha}{d+1}. \end{equation} Since $r'>1$ and $r'-\delta>1$, we have $1<r'(r'-\delta)$ and {\rm (\ref{const22})} is satisfied whenever $$ \delta \leq \frac{\delta }{4(d+1)}+\frac{\alpha}{d+1}, \qquad \textrm{that is} \qquad \delta \leq \frac{\alpha (4d+1)}{(d+1)(4d+3)}. $$ Setting finally $$ \delta= \min \left( \frac{\alpha (4d+1)}{(d+1)(4d+3)},\frac{r'-1}{2} \right), $$ we verify that all constraints are satisfied. This concludes the estimation of the term $R_{t,3}$ and yields {\rm (\ref{R3})}. Regarding $R_{t,4}$, we use once more the Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality to obtain, for the same $q',\varepsilon$ and $s$ as above and $s_0=\frac{sd}{d+s(\alpha+\varepsilon)}<s$, $$ \|R_{t,4}\|_{L^{q'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \leq C\| t^{-\varepsilon} (1+|x|) u_t \|_{L^{q'}(\mathbb R_t,L^{s_0}(\mathbb R_x^{d}))} \leq C\| t^{-\varepsilon} u_t \|_{L^{q'}(\mathbb R_t,L^{s}(\mathbb R_x^{d}))} $$ since $u_t$ has a compact support in $x$. It then suffices to proceed as for $R_{t,3}$. Finally, as already mentioned, the term $R_{t,2}$ is more regular and is treated with a similar and simpler analysis. This then enables us to estimate $I_0$ by $$ \|I_0\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)} \leq C \|\phi_t\|_{L^{r'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})}, $$ under the condition {\rm (\ref{mainconst})}. We turn now to the term $I_2$. \paragraph{The term $I_2$.} We start with the following lemma. \begin{lemma} Let $\varphi \in \mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d})$, and let $\alpha,\beta>0$ with $\alpha+\beta<1$. Then, for any $\varepsilon>0$, we have the estimate $$ \left\| \big[1+|x|^\alpha,\Lambda_{\alpha+\beta}\big] \varphi \right \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^{d})} \leq C \| \varphi \|_{H^{\beta+\varepsilon}(\mathbb R^d)}.$$ \end{lemma} \begin{proof} We proceed in the Fourier space. First, the Fourier transform of $|x|^\alpha$ reads, see \cite{gelfand}, section 3.3, $$ \mathcal F_x(|x|^\alpha)(\xi)= C_{\alpha,d} |\xi|^{-d-\alpha}, \qquad C_{\alpha,d}= 2^{\alpha+d} \pi^{\frac{d}{2}} \frac{\Gamma(\frac{\alpha+d}{2})}{\Gamma(-\frac{\alpha}{2})}. $$ Therefore, \begin{eqnarray*} \mathcal F_x \left(\big[1+|x|^\alpha,\Lambda_{\alpha+\beta}\big ]\varphi\right)(\xi)&=&C_{\alpha,d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} \frac{(1+|k|^2)^{(\alpha+\beta)/2}-(1+|\xi|^2)^{(\alpha+\beta)/2}}{|\xi-k|^{d+\alpha}} \mathcal F_x \varphi(k) dk\\ &:=&F(\xi). \end{eqnarray*} Since the function $ \mathbb R \ni u \mapsto (1+u^2)^{\gamma/2}$ is of H\"older regularity $\gamma$ for $\gamma \in (0,1)$, there exists a constant $C$ such that $$ |(1+|k|^2)^{(\alpha+\beta)/2}-(1+|\xi|^2)^{(\alpha+\beta)/2}| \leq C||k|-|\xi||^{\alpha+\beta} \leq C |k-\xi|^{\alpha+\beta}. $$ Hence, $F$ can be estimated by $$ |F(\xi)|\leq C \int_{\mathbb R^d} \frac{|\mathcal F_x \varphi(k)| }{|\xi-k|^{d-\beta}} dk. $$ Using the estimate {\rm (\ref{riesz})} on Riesz potentials, we find, together with the H\"older inequality for the second line, \begin{eqnarray*} \|F\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)} &\leq& C \| \mathcal F_x \varphi\|_{L^{\frac{2d}{d+2\beta}}(\mathbb R^d)}\\ &\leq & C \|(1+|\xi|^{(\frac{\beta+\varepsilon}{\beta})d})^{-1}\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^d)} \| (1+|\xi|^{\beta+\varepsilon})\mathcal F_x \varphi\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb R^d)}\\[2mm] &\leq & C \| (1+|\xi|^{\beta+\varepsilon})\mathcal F_x \varphi\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb R^d)}. \end{eqnarray*} This concludes the proof of the lemma. \end{proof} \medskip With the latter lemma at hand, the estimation of $I_2$ is now straightforward: we have, for any $\varepsilon>0$, \begin{eqnarray*} \|I_2\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}&=&\left\|\big[1+|x|^\alpha,\Lambda_{\alpha+\beta}\big] \int_{\mathbb R } dt e^{-i t \Delta} u_t \right\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}\\ & \leq& C \left\| \Lambda_{\beta+\varepsilon} \int_{\mathbb R } dt e^{-i t \Delta} u_t \right\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)}\\ &\leq & C \| \phi_t\|_{L^{r'}(\mathbb R^d)}, \end{eqnarray*} where we used Theorem \ref{thCS} in the last line with $$ \beta+\varepsilon < \frac{d+1}{r}-\frac{d}{2}, \qquad r'\in[1,2), \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \beta+\alpha \leq \frac{1}{2}, \qquad r'=2. $$ With for instance $\varepsilon=\alpha$, the latter condition is implied by {\rm (\ref{mainconst})}. Note as well that the relation above implies $\beta \leq 1/2$, so that with the fact that $\alpha \leq 1/4$ according to the hypotheses of Lemma \ref{pr1}, we have $\alpha+\beta<1$ and Lemma \ref{com} can indeed be applied. In order to conclude the proof of Lemma \ref{pr1}, it remains to treat the term $I_1$, which is a direct consequence of Theorem \ref{thCS}. This ends the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Split into $I_0$ (weight term), $I_1$ and a commutator $I_2$; handle $I_0$ via the commutation $|x|^\alpha e^{-it\Delta}=e^{-it\Delta}A^\alpha_t$ and Theorem 2.1. The key step bounds the remainder $R_{t,3}$ by Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev with a careful choice of exponents.

nodes.name: Commutator estimate for 1+|x|^alpha and Lambda_{alpha+beta}
nodes.statement: Let $\varphi \in \mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d})$, and let $\alpha,\beta>0$ with $\alpha+\beta<1$. Then, for any $\varepsilon>0$, we have the estimate $$ \left\| \big[1+|x|^\alpha,\Lambda_{\alpha+\beta}\big] \varphi \right \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^{d})} \leq C \| \varphi \|_{H^{\beta+\varepsilon}(\mathbb R^d)}.$$
conclusions: we have the estimate $$ \left\| \big[1+|x|^\alpha,\Lambda_{\alpha+\beta}\big] \varphi \right \|_{L^2(\mathbb R^{d})} \leq C \| \varphi \|_{H^{\beta+\varepsilon}(\mathbb R^d)}.$$
nodes.label: com

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: We proceed in the Fourier space. First, the Fourier transform of $|x|^\alpha$ reads, see \cite{gelfand}, section 3.3, $$ \mathcal F_x(|x|^\alpha)(\xi)= C_{\alpha,d} |\xi|^{-d-\alpha}, \qquad C_{\alpha,d}= 2^{\alpha+d} \pi^{\frac{d}{2}} \frac{\Gamma(\frac{\alpha+d}{2})}{\Gamma(-\frac{\alpha}{2})}. $$ Therefore, \begin{eqnarray*} \mathcal F_x \left(\big[1+|x|^\alpha,\Lambda_{\alpha+\beta}\big ]\varphi\right)(\xi)&=&C_{\alpha,d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} \frac{(1+|k|^2)^{(\alpha+\beta)/2}-(1+|\xi|^2)^{(\alpha+\beta)/2}}{|\xi-k|^{d+\alpha}} \mathcal F_x \varphi(k) dk\\ &:=&F(\xi). \end{eqnarray*} Since the function $ \mathbb R \ni u \mapsto (1+u^2)^{\gamma/2}$ is of H\"older regularity $\gamma$ for $\gamma \in (0,1)$, there exists a constant $C$ such that $$ |(1+|k|^2)^{(\alpha+\beta)/2}-(1+|\xi|^2)^{(\alpha+\beta)/2}| \leq C||k|-|\xi||^{\alpha+\beta} \leq C |k-\xi|^{\alpha+\beta}. $$ Hence, $F$ can be estimated by $$ |F(\xi)|\leq C \int_{\mathbb R^d} \frac{|\mathcal F_x \varphi(k)| }{|\xi-k|^{d-\beta}} dk. $$ Using the estimate {\rm (\ref{riesz})} on Riesz potentials, we find, together with the H\"older inequality for the second line, \begin{eqnarray*} \|F\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)} &\leq& C \| \mathcal F_x \varphi\|_{L^{\frac{2d}{d+2\beta}}(\mathbb R^d)}\\ &\leq & C \|(1+|\xi|^{(\frac{\beta+\varepsilon}{\beta})d})^{-1}\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^d)} \| (1+|\xi|^{\beta+\varepsilon})\mathcal F_x \varphi\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb R^d)}\\[2mm] &\leq & C \| (1+|\xi|^{\beta+\varepsilon})\mathcal F_x \varphi\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb R^d)}. \end{eqnarray*} This concludes the proof of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Fourier side: Holder regularity of $(1+u^2)^{\gamma/2}$ reduces the commutator to a Riesz potential, then Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev and Holder.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.5
nodes.statement: As in the proof of Theorem \ref{th1}, we focus on $n_{\gamma_\beta}$, and consider a nonnegative finite rank ``smooth'' operator $\varrho$ verifying {\rm (\ref{condrho})}, the final estimates following by density. This will justify the formal calculations. In this setting, we have in particular that $\Gamma (t) \in \mathcal J_1$ and $(\mu_j(t))^{1/2}\phi_j(t) \in \mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ for all $t \in \mathbb R$, for $(\mu_j,\phi_j)_{p\in \mathbb N}$ the spectral decomposition of $\Gamma$. For $v\in C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, let then $$ n^v(t,x):=|v(x)|^2 n_{\Gamma}(t,x)=\sum_{j\in \mathbb N} \mu_j(t) |\phi^v_j(t,x)|^2, \qquad \phi^v_j:=v \phi_j. $$ The proof consists in applying $D^\beta$ to $n^v$ and in using the estimates of Theorem \ref{th1}. This requires some care since there is no simple product rule for the fractional derivative. Let $\varphi \in \mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. Then, with the local representation of the fractional Laplacian {\rm (\ref{locfrac})} and the identity $|a|^2-|b|^2= 2\Re\, (a-b)(\overline{a}+\overline{b})$, we find, for $\beta \in (0,1/2]$, \begin{eqnarray*} D^\beta(|\varphi|^2)(x)&=&c_{d,\beta} \int_{\mathbb R^d} \frac{|\varphi(x)|^2-|\varphi(y)|^2}{|x-y|^{d+\beta}}dy\\ &=&2 c_{d,\beta} \Re\int_{\mathbb R^d} \frac{(\varphi(x)-\varphi(y))(\overline{\varphi(y)}-\overline{\varphi(x)}+2\overline{\varphi(x)} )}{|x-y|^{d+\beta}}dy\\[2mm] &=&4 \Re \; \overline{\varphi} D^\beta(\varphi)(x)-2 c_{d,\beta} |\mathcal D_{\beta/2}\varphi|^2, \end{eqnarray*} where $$ \mathcal D_{\beta/2}(\varphi)=\left(\int_{\mathbb R^d} \frac{|\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)|^2}{|x-y|^{d+\beta}}dy\right)^{1/2}. $$ Replacing $\varphi$ by $ (\mu_j(t))^{1/2}\phi_j^v(t)$, we obtain the following expression of $D^\beta n^v$: $$ D^\beta n^v= 4 \Re \, \sum_{j\in \mathbb N} \mu_j\overline{\phi^v_j} D^\beta(\phi^v_j)-2 c_{d,\beta} \, \sum_{j\in \mathbb N} \mu_j |\mathcal D_{\beta/2}(\phi^v_j)|^2. $$ The first term of the r.h.s. can be thought of as the most singular term, and can be treated with Theorem \ref{th1} after some technicalities. An important point is the fact that we do not use the triangle inequality for the estimation, and therefore the fact that the $\phi_j$'s are orthogonal is directly exploited. The second term is more critical. To the best of our knowledge, there are not many ways to estimate $\mathcal D_{\beta/2}(\phi^v_j)$, and one is given in \cite{stein1}, Theorem 1, and provides controls of the $L^p$ norm of $\mathcal D_{\beta/2}(\phi_j^v)$ in terms of the $L^p$ norm of $\Lambda_{\beta/2}\phi^v_j$. This means that we need to use the triangle inequality at this stage. This does not imply that the orthogonality of the $\phi_p$'s is not used at all, it is when we invoke Theorem \ref{th1} when $r=2$ in the case $p>1$. These latter facts explain the limitation to the $L^1$ norm in time. The results could be extended to higher norms in time if we were able to replace $\Lambda_\beta$ by $\mathcal D_{\beta}$ in the definition of $\gamma_\beta$, and prove an analog to Theorem \ref{th1}. This does not seem trivial since $\mathcal D_{\beta}$ is not linear. Using therefore the Cauchy-Schwarz and triangle inequalities, we find \begin{eqnarray} \nonumber \|D^\beta n^v\|_{L^{\frac{d}{d-\beta}}(\mathbb R_x^d)}&\leq& C \left\| \left(\sum_{j\in \mathbb N} \mu_j |\phi^v_j|^2\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_{j\in \mathbb N} \mu_j |D^\beta(\phi^v_j)|^2\right)^{1/2} \right\|_{L^{\frac{d}{d-\beta}}(\mathbb R^d_x)}\\ && \qquad +C \sum_{j\in \mathbb N} \mu_j\big\|\mathcal D_{\beta/2}(\phi_j^v) \big\|_{L^{\frac{2d}{d-\beta}}(\mathbb R^d_x)}^2. \end{eqnarray} Thanks to \cite{stein1}, Theorem 1, we can control the term in $\mathcal D_{\beta/2}(\phi_j^v)$ by (remark that obviously $2d/(d+\beta)<2d/(d-\beta)$), $$ \|\mathcal D_{\beta/2}(\phi_j^v) \big\|_{L^{\frac{2d}{d-\beta}}(\mathbb R^d_x)} \leq C \|\Lambda_{\beta/2} \phi_j^v\|_{L^{\frac{2d}{d-\beta}}(\mathbb R^d_x)} \leq C \|\Lambda_{\beta} \phi_j^v\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb R^d_x)}, $$ where we used the Sobolev embedding $H^{\beta/2,2}(\mathbb R^d) \subset L^{\frac{2d}{d-\beta}}(\mathbb R^d)$ for the second inequality. Furthermore, using the H\"older inequality and the embedding $H^{\beta,2}(\mathbb R^d) \subset L^{\frac{2d}{d-2\beta}}(\mathbb R^d)$ for the first term in the r.h.s of {\rm (\ref{Dn})}, we find \begin{eqnarray*} \|D^\beta n^v\|_{L^{\frac{d}{d-\beta}}(\mathbb R_x^d)}&\leq& C \sum_{j\in \mathbb N} \mu_j \left( \|\Lambda^\beta(\phi^v_j)\|^2_{L^2(\mathbb R_x^d)}+\|D^\beta(\phi^v_j)\|^2_{L^2(\mathbb R_x^d)}\right)\\ &\leq & C \sum_{j\in \mathbb N} \mu_j \left( \|\phi^v_j\|^2_{L^2(\mathbb R^d_x)}+\|D^\beta(\phi^v_j)\|^2_{L^2(\mathbb R_x^d)} \right). \end{eqnarray*} Above, we used \cite{stein1}, Theorem 2, in order to estimate $\Lambda_\beta$ in terms of $D^\beta$. We control now $D^\beta( v \phi_p)$ in terms of $v D^\beta(\phi_p)$. We have, for all $\varphi \in \mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, \begin{eqnarray*} D^\beta(v \varphi)(x)&=&c_{d,\beta} \int_{\mathbb R^d} \frac{v(x)\varphi(x)-v(y)\varphi(y)}{|x-y|^{d+\beta}}dy\\ &=&c_{d,\beta} \int_{\mathbb R^d} \frac{v(x)(\varphi(x)-\varphi(y))+(v(x)-v(y))\varphi(y)}{|x-y|^{d+\beta}}dy\\ &=&v(x)D^\beta(\varphi)(x)+c_{d,\beta} \int_{\mathbb R^d} \frac{v(x)-v(y)}{|x-y|^{d+\beta}}\varphi(y) dy. \end{eqnarray*} Supposing that the support of $v$ is compactly embedded in a bounded set $\Omega$, we write the last term above as $$ c_{d,\beta} \int_{\Omega} \frac{v(x)-v(y)}{|x-y|^{d+\beta}}\varphi(y) dy+c_{d,\beta} v(x)\int_{\Omega^c} \frac{\varphi(y)}{|x-y|^{d+\beta}} dy. $$ Hence, \begin{align*} & \sum_{j\in \mathbb N} \mu_j(t) \|D^\beta(\phi^v_j(t,\cdot))\|^2_{L^2(\mathbb R^d_x)}=\left\| \sum_{j\in \mathbb N} \mu_j(t) |D^\beta(\phi^v_j(t,\cdot))|^2 \right\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^d_x)}\\ &\hspace{1.8cm} \leq C \left\| \sum_{j\in \mathbb N} \mu_j(t) |v D^\beta(\phi_j(t,\cdot))|^2 \right\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^d_x)}+C\left\| N_1(t,\cdot) \right\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^d_x)}+C\left\| N_2(t,\cdot) \right\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^d_x)}, \end{align*} where we have defined \begin{eqnarray*} N_1(t,x)&:=&\sum_{j\in \mathbb N} \mu_j(t)\left|\int_{\Omega} \frac{v(x)-v(y)}{|x-y|^{d+\beta}}\phi_j(t,y) dy \right|^2\\ N_2(t,x)&:=& \sum_{j\in \mathbb N} \mu_j(t)\left|v(x)\int_{\Omega^c} \frac{\phi_j(t,y)}{|x-y|^{d+\beta}} dy \right|^2. \end{eqnarray*} Writing the squares above as the product of two integrals, and using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality lead to $$ N_1(t,x) \leq \left|\int_{\Omega} \frac{|v(x)-v(y)|}{|x-y|^{d+\beta}} (n_{\Gamma}(t,y))^{1/2} dy \right|^2, \quad N_2(t,x) \leq |v(x)|^2 \left|\int_{\Omega^c} \frac{(n_{\Gamma}(t,y))^{1/2} }{|x-y|^{d+\beta}} dy \right|^2. $$ Using the estimate {\rm (\ref{riesz})} on Riesz potentials and the fact that $|v(x)-v(y)|\leq C |x-y|$, we find, when $d\geq 2$, \begin{eqnarray*} \left\| N_1(t,\cdot) \right\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^d_x)} &\leq& C \int_{\mathbb R^d} \left|\int_{\Omega} \frac{(n_{\Gamma}(t,y))^{1/2} }{|x-y|^{d+\beta-1}} dy \right|^2 dx\\[2mm] & \leq &C \|n_{\Gamma}(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{\frac{d}{d+2(1-\beta)}}(\Omega)} \leq C \|n_{\Gamma}(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)}. \end{eqnarray*} When $d=1$, {\rm (\ref{riesz})} cannot be used as above. We then control $|v(x)-v(y)|$ instead by $|v(x)-v(y)|\leq C |x-y|^{1/2}$, and since $\beta \in (0,\frac{1}{2}]$, we can apply {\rm (\ref{riesz})} and obtain $$ \left\| N_1(t,\cdot) \right\|_{L^1(\mathbb R_x)} \leq C \|n_{\Gamma}(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{\frac{1}{1+2(1/2-\beta)}}(\Omega)} \leq C \|n_{\Gamma}(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)}. $$ Regarding $N_2$, for $x \in \textrm{supp } v \subset \subset \Omega$ and $y \in \Omega^c$, there exists a constant $C$ such that $|x-y|^{-1} \leq C (1+|y|)^{-1}$, and therefore $$ \left\| N_2(t,\cdot) \right\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^d_x)} \leq C \|n_{\Gamma}(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{q}(\mathbb R^d_x)}, \qquad \forall q\in[1,\infty]. $$ It remains to bound $n_{\Gamma}$. Note that according to the last estimate, this has to be done over $\mathbb R^d$ and not just on a bounded domain, and this is a consequence of the non-locality of the fractional derivative. Estimating $n_{\Gamma}$ is not trivial unless $\varrho$ is trace class so that the triangle inequality can be used. When $\varrho$ is not trace class, the orthogonality of the eigenfunctions plays again a crucial role, and we then use the Strichartz estimates of \cite{FrankSabin}, Theorem 15, to obtain $$ \|n_{\Gamma} \|_{L^{\frac{p'}{d}}(-T,T,L^{\frac{p}{2-p}}(\mathbb R^d))} \leq C \|\varrho \|_{L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_p)}, \qquad p \in [1,2d/(2d-1)]. $$ We verify indeed that our choice of parameters above satisfy the assumptions of the theorem of \cite{FrankSabin}, using in particular that $p'>2d$ when $\beta \geq 0$. Collecting all previous estimates, we find $$ \|D^{\beta}(n^v) \|_{L^1(-T,T,L^{\frac{d}{d-\beta}}(\mathbb R^d))} \leq C \left\| \sum_{j\in \mathbb N} \mu_j |v D^\beta(\phi_j)|^2 \right\|_{L^1((-T,T) \times \mathbb R^d)} + C \|\varrho \|_{L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_p)} $$ and conclude by controlling the first term in r.h.s. using Theorem \ref{th1} with $r=2$ and $\beta$ satisfying the conditions stated in the corollary. This ends the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Expand $D^\beta(|v\phi_j|^2)$ by the integral formula for the fractional Laplacian, control the leading term with Theorem 2.4 ($r=2$) and the remainder with Stein's square function bounds and Strichartz estimates.

nodes.name: Plan of the proof
nodes.statement: The proof is an application of Theorem \ref{thCS} and Lemma \ref{pr1}. We focus on the term $\gamma_\beta$ and explain at the end of the proof the straighforward adaptation to $\sigma_\beta$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 2.1 and Lemma 2.7; treat $\gamma_\beta$, then adapt to $\sigma_\beta$.

nodes.name: Reduction to nonnegative rho
nodes.statement: We remark first that we can limit ourselves to nonnegative operators $\varrho$ in $\mathcal J_p$, $p<\infty$. We can indeed decompose $\varrho$ as $\varrho=\varrho_+-\varrho_-$, $\varrho_{\pm} \geq 0$, $\varrho_+ \varrho_-=\varrho_- \varrho_+=0$, and the linearity of the trace yields $$ |n_{\gamma_\beta}|=|n_{\gamma_{+,\beta}}-n_{\gamma_{-,\beta}}| \leq n_{\gamma_{+,\beta}}+n_{\gamma_{-,\beta}}. $$ It suffices then to apply the estimates that we will derive for $n_{\gamma_{\pm,\beta}}$, together with $$ \| \varrho_{\pm} \|_{\mathcal J_p} \leq \|\varrho\|_{\mathcal J_p}, \qquad p \in [1,\infty). $$
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $\varrho\ge0$ via $\varrho=\varrho_+-\varrho_-$.

nodes.name: Reduction to smooth finite-rank rho
nodes.statement: Also, in order to justify some formal computations, we consider ``smooth'' operators $\varrho$ satisfying the following conditions: $\varrho$ is finite rank and \begin{equation} \int_{\mathbb R} dt\, \textrm{Tr} \Big((1+|x|^k) (-\Delta)^n \,\varrho(t)\, (-\Delta)^n (1+|x|^k)\Big) <\infty, \quad \forall k,n \in \mathbb N. \end{equation} The final estimates are then obtained by density since such operators are dense in $L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_p)$, $p<\infty$: on the one hand finite rank operators are dense in $\mathcal J_p$, $p<\infty$, and on the other, we have, for any smooth cut-off $\chi_\eta$ with $\chi_\eta(x) \to 1$ pointwise as $\eta \to 0$, $$ \chi_\eta e^{\eta \Delta}\, \varrho \, e^{\eta \Delta} \chi_\eta \to \varrho \qquad \textrm{in} \quad L^1(\mathbb R_+,\mathcal J_p) \qquad \textrm{as} \qquad \eta \to 0, $$ whenever $\varrho \in L^1(\mathbb R,\mathcal J_p)$, $p\in [1,\infty]$. The regularity of $\varrho$ is then propagated to the operator $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^t e^{i (t-s) \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{-i (t-s) \Delta} ds$, see e.g. \cite{cazenave}, section 2.5, and as a consequence $\Gamma$ verifies $$ \sup_{t \in \mathbb R} \textrm{Tr} \Big((1+|x|^k) (-\Delta)^n \,\Gamma(t)\, (-\Delta)^n (1+|x|^k)\Big) <\infty, \quad \forall k,n \in \mathbb N. $$ In particular, if $(\mu_j,\phi_j)_{j\in \mathbb N}$ is the spectral decomposition of $\Gamma$, this shows that $$ \sup_{t \in \mathbb R} \sum_{j \in \mathbb N} \mu_j(t) \left\|(1+|x|^k) (-\Delta)^n \,\phi_j(t)\right\|^2_{L^2(\mathbb R^d)} < \infty, \quad \forall k,n \in \mathbb N, $$ and therefore $(\mu_j(t))^{1/2}\phi_j(t) \in \mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ for all $t \in \mathbb R$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce by density to smooth finite-rank $\varrho$, whose regularity propagates to $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.1 and its proof
nodes.statement: The proof starts with the following lemma: \begin{lemma} Let $\beta \in [0,1/2]$. For any $\varphi\in C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})$, the following relation holds: $$ \int_{\mathbb R} \int_{\mathbb R^d} dt dx\, n_{\gamma_\beta}(t,x) \varphi(t,x) =\int_{\mathbb R} ds \textrm{Tr} \, \big( e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{is \Delta} F_\beta(s) \big), $$ where $$ F_\beta(s)=\int_{|s|}^\infty dt \, \Lambda_{\beta}e^{-i t \Delta }f_t e^{i t \Delta } \Lambda_{\beta} \in C^0(\mathbb R,\mathcal L(L^2(\mathbb R^d))), \qquad f_t=\chi_t \varphi_t \chi_t. $$ \end{lemma} \begin{proof} We begin with the following equalities, supposing that the support in $t$ of $\chi_t$ is included on $[-T,T]$: \begin{eqnarray*} \int_{\mathbb R} \int_{\mathbb R^d} dt dx \, n_{\gamma_\beta(t)}(t,x) \varphi(t,x) &=& \int_{-T}^T dt \, \textrm{Tr} \big( \gamma_\beta(t) \varphi_t \big)\\ &=&\int_{-T}^T dt \,\textrm{Tr} \left( \chi_t \Lambda_{\beta} \int_0^t ds e^{i(t- s) \Delta} \varrho(s) e^{-i (t-s) \Delta }\Lambda_{\beta} \chi_t \, \varphi_t ds \right)\\ &=&\int_{-T}^T \int_0^t ds dt \, \textrm{Tr} \Big( \chi_t \Lambda_{\beta}e^{i(t- s) \Delta} \varrho(s)e^{-i (t-s) \Delta }\Lambda_{\beta}\chi_t \, \varphi_t \Big)\\[2mm] &:=&I. \end{eqnarray*} The last equality is justified by \begin{align} &\int_0^t ds \,\left|\textrm{Tr} \left( \chi_t \Lambda_{\beta}e^{i(t- s) \Delta} \varrho(s)e^{-i (t-s) \Delta }\Lambda_{\beta}\chi_t \, \varphi_t \right)\right| \\ \nonumber &\hspace{2cm}=\int_0^t ds \,\left|\textrm{Tr} \left( \chi_t e^{i(t- s) \Delta} \Lambda_{\beta} \varrho(s)\Lambda_{\beta} e^{-i (t-s) \Delta }\chi_t \, \varphi_t \right)\right| \\ \nonumber &\hspace{2cm} \leq \|\chi_t\|^2_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \|\varphi_t \|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^{d+1})} \int_{\mathbb R} ds\, \| \Lambda_{\beta} \varrho(s) \Lambda_{\beta} \|_{\mathcal J_1} < \infty. \end{align} Above, we used the fact that $\Lambda_\beta$ and $e^{it \Delta}$ commute. Since the operator $\Lambda_\beta$ is not bounded, we need an additional step to justify the use of the cyclicity of the trace and to obtain that $$ I=\int_{-T}^T ds\,\textrm{Tr} \left( e^{-i s \Delta} \varrho(s)e^{i s \Delta } \Lambda_{\beta} \int_{|s|}^\infty dt e^{-i t \Delta} f_t e^{i t \Delta} \Lambda_{\beta} \right), $$ which would end the proof. We therefore regularize $I$ as $$ I_\eta=\int_{-T}^T \int_0^tds dt\, \textrm{Tr} \left( \chi_t \Lambda^\eta \Lambda_{\beta} e^{i(t- s) \Delta} \varrho(s)e^{-i (t-s) \Delta }\Lambda_{\beta} \Lambda^\eta \chi_t \, \varphi_t \right), $$ where $\Lambda^\eta=(\mathbb{I}-\eta \Delta)^{-1}$. Similar estimates as in {\rm (\ref{justi})} show that $I_\eta \to I$ as $\eta \to 0$.
